predictors.name: ColabFold (sokrypton/ColabFold) + the api.colabfold.com MSA server
predictors.paper: Mirdita et al., "ColabFold: making protein folding accessible to all", Nature Methods 2022 (title confirmed via Crossref)
predictors.code_licence: MIT — VERIFIED by fetching LICENSE ("MIT License, Copyright (c) 2021 Sergey Ovchinnikov").
predictors.weights_licence: ColabFold ships no weights of its own; it runs AlphaFold2 weights (CC BY 4.0, commercial OK) and optionally AlphaFold2-multimer. Licence status therefore follows AF2: clean for commercial use with attribution.

predictors.runtime_estimate: MSA step MEASURED BY ME on this machine: 63-residue query, submit -> COMPLETE in approximately 50 s (10 polls x 5 s), 542 KB gzip returned. Folding step: not run (no CUDA). No published CPU folding timing; I will not invent one.
predictors.api_endpoint: https://api.colabfold.com — TESTED END-TO-END BY ME TODAY, WORKS. Contract read from colabfold/colabfold.py run_mmseqs2(): POST https://api.colabfold.com/ticket/msa with FORM-URLENCODED body (NOT multipart) fields q=<FASTA text> and mode=<env|all|nofilter|...>; use /ticket/pair instead of /ticket/msa for paired multimer MSAs. Returns {"id":"...","status":"PENDING"}. Poll GET /ticket/{id} until status==COMPLETE (statuses seen: PENDING, RUNNING, COMPLETE, ERROR). Then GET /result/download/{id} -> gzipped tar. Templates: GET /template/{line}.
predictors.api_limits: MEASURED: HTTP 200 on submit, ~50 s to COMPLETE, 542,027-byte tar.gz containing uniref.a3m, bfd.mgnify30.metaeuk30.smag30.a3m, pdb70.m8, msa.sh. The uniref.a3m held 6,153 sequences. The client sets a User-Agent header and the upstream source implements 5 s backoff plus automatic resubmission, which implies server-side throttling. I did NOT retrieve a documented numeric rate limit or per-day cap — do not assume one exists in your favour. This is a free academic service run by the Steinegger/Söding groups; a production pipeline should set a descriptive User-Agent, serialise requests, and be prepared to self-host the MMseqs2 server.

predictors.name: ESM Atlas hosted fold API (esmatlas.com) — ESMFold v1
predictors.paper: Lin et al., "Evolutionary-scale prediction of atomic-level protein structure with a language model", Science 2023 (title confirmed via Crossref)
predictors.code_licence: n/a (hosted service). Underlying esm repo is MIT.
predictors.weights_licence: n/a to the caller. The returned PDB embeds this REMARK, which I read in the actual response body: "ESM METAGENOMIC ATLAS DATA IS AVAILABLE UNDER A CC-BY-4.0 LICENSE FOR ACADEMIC AND COMMERCIAL USE." So returned coordinates are CC-BY-4.0, commercial use permitted.
predictors.hardware_minimum: None — it is an HTTP call. This is exactly the shape of thing the platform wants. The problem is that it no longer computes.
predictors.runtime_estimate: Cache hits: 0.10-0.33 s (measured, 3 consecutive runs). Novel sequences: NEVER COMPLETES — 504 at either 10 s (CloudFront) or 29 s (API Gateway).
predictors.api_endpoint: https://api.esmatlas.com/foldSequence/v1/pdb/ — POST, raw amino-acid string as the request body (no JSON, no form encoding). The page at esmatlas.com/resources?action=fold is a JS single-page app (VERIFIED HTTP 200, but the body is an empty React root, so nothing is scrapable from it).
predictors.api_limits: HARD FINDING — THE API IS ALIVE AT THE GATEWAY BUT ITS INFERENCE BACKEND IS DEAD. Exact HTTP responses I got today: (a) validation layer works perfectly and instantly — 401 residues -> HTTP 413 body "Sequence is longer than 400."; 400 residues -> passes validation; empty body -> HTTP 400 "Sequence is empty."; bad characters -> HTTP 422 "Sequence is only allowed to have {C,W,T,D,B,N,Q,J,P,I,L,A,X,H,E,Z,Y,F,R,V,K,M,G,S} tokens."; GET instead of POST -> HTTP 403 "Missing Authentication Token". So THE SEQUENCE-LENGTH CAP IS EXACTLY 400 RESIDUES, server-enforced, confirmed by bisection at the 400/401 boundary. (b) BUT actual folding never returns. I sent novel random sequences at lengths 10, 20, 30, 50, 80, 120, 200 — ALL returned HTTP 504 ("Gateway Time-out" at 10 s, or {"message": "Endpoint request timed out"} at 29 s). A 30-mer failed 4/4 times. The ONLY 200 I ever got was for the trivial string MKTVRQERLK, which returned in 0.105-0.326 s across three repeats — far too fast for inference, i.e. a cached result from an earlier user. Conclusion: only pre-cached sequences succeed; anything novel times out. No rate-limit headers are exposed (response headers are plain AWS API Gateway: x-amzn-requestid, x-amz-apigw-id, access-control-allow-methods: OPTIONS,POST). VERDICT: DO NOT BUILD ON THIS. It will pass a naive health check and a naive cached-sequence smoke test, then fail on every real user query.
outputs: A raw PDB text body (not JSON). HEADER line dated 18-OCT-22, TITLE "ESMFOLD V1 PREDICTION FOR INPUT", REMARK block citing Lin et al. and the CC-BY-4.0 licence.

Confidence: pLDDT is written into the B-factor column, PER-ATOM, and CRITICALLY ON A 0-1 SCALE, NOT 0-100. I verified this in the returned body: residue 1 atoms N/CA/C/CB/O carry 0.83/0.82/0.83/0.78/0.76 — distinct per atom, all sub-1.0. A parser that assumes the usual 0-100 AlphaFold convention will silently report every model as ~1% confident.
NO PAE, NO pTM, NO ipTM, NO ranking_score, NO has_clash are returned by this endpoint. pLDDT in the B-factor column is the entire confidence signal.

The official `pip install "fair-esm[esmfold]"` route is IMPOSSIBLE on macOS: it pulls in aqlaboratory/openfold, and the esm README states verbatim "Openfold installation requires `nvcc`" — there is no nvcc on a Mac. Writing via the convenience PDB writer puts pLDDT in the B-factor column.

WHAT ESMFOLD EMITS INSTEAD OF THE AF3 SET: it gives pLDDT and pTM and a PAE matrix, but it has NO ipTM, NO ranking_score, NO has_clash, and NO affinity. There is no interface metric because the model is fundamentally single-chain.

Scale warning: the hosted API emits 0-1 pLDDT (I verified that directly). Do not assume the local path uses the same scale as the API — normalise explicitly and assert the range at parse time rather than trusting either.

affinity_[input].json — fields, verbatim: affinity_pred_value, affinity_probability_binary, affinity_pred_value1, affinity_probability_binary1, affinity_pred_value2, affinity_probability_binary2

UNITS, transcribed from the README: affinity_pred_value "reports a binding affinity value as log10(IC50), derived from an IC50 measured in uM". affinity_probability_binary is a 0-1 probability that the ligand is a binder.

USAGE SPLIT stated by the authors: use affinity_probability_binary to separate binders from decoys at hit-discovery stage; use affinity_pred_value for hit-to-lead / lead-optimisation ranking. They are trained on largely different datasets with different supervision — do not average them.

DOCUMENTED LIMITS on the affinity head: exactly one small-molecule ligand chain per job; at most 128 heavy+retained atoms after RDKit RemoveHs; authors do not recommend ligands much above 56 atoms (the training limit). Protein targets only — RNA/DNA/cofactor targets "will not crash but the output will be unreliable".

structure.recommendation:
RECOMMENDATION — what to actually ship on a GPU-less MacBook, and what to refuse to claim.

MACHINE REALITY CHECK FIRST. The premise "no discrete GPU" is true but slightly misleading here. This is an Apple M5 Max, 18 cores, 128 GB unified memory, macOS 26.5.2, torch 2.13.0 with MPS available and CUDA false. There is no CUDA, but there IS a capable Metal GPU and more addressable memory than an A100 80GB. The binding constraint is the CUDA/Linux ecosystem, not compute or RAM.

TIER 1 — WORKS TODAY, VERIFIED BY ME, COMMERCIALLY CLEAN.
1. ColabFold MSA server. I ran the full round trip today: POST https://api.colabfold.com/ticket/msa (form-urlencoded q= and mode=, NOT multipart — my first attempt with multipart returned HTTP 400 "http: no such file"), poll GET /ticket/{id}, then GET /result/download/{id}. A 63-residue query completed in ~50 s and returned a 542 KB tar.gz containing uniref.a3m with 6,153 sequences. Zero GPU. MIT client, AF2 weights CC BY 4.0. This is the single most valuable working component available to the platform.
2. ESMFold locally via HuggingFace transformers. MIT code, MIT weights, 8.4 GB fp32 (verified via x-linked-size), fits trivially in 128 GB. The critical routing decision: the official `pip install "fair-esm[esmfold]"` path is IMPOSSIBLE on macOS because it pulls aqlaboratory/openfold and the esm README states "Openfold installation requires `nvcc`". The HuggingFace path sidesteps this entirely — transformers vendors openfold_utils as pure Python and modeling_esmfold.py contains zero nvcc/CUDAExtension references. Use transformers, never fair-esm[esmfold], on this machine.
3. OpenFold3 via the NVIDIA endpoint, or locally on MPS. Apache 2.0 for code, weights AND training data — the only fully-open AF3-class stack.

TIER 2 — WORKS BUT NEEDS ONE SETUP STEP.
Boltz-2 is the best licence in the set (MIT for code and weights, commercial use, no gate, plus a binding-affinity head). Its CPU path is officially supported and the CUDA kernels are optional extras. But there is a hard blocker I verified: boltz 2.2.1 requires_python "<3.13,>=3.10" and the only interpreter on this machine is 3.14.6 (no 3.10-3.13, no conda, no uv). You must install a Python 3.12 before `pip install boltz` will resolve. I did not do this unprompted since it modifies the user's environment — flagging it as the one action needed to unlock Boltz.

TIER 3 — ELIMINATED, WITH PROOF.
- Protenix: cannot install. It has 32 HARD (non-extra) dependencies including triton==3.3.1 and cuequivariance-ops-torch-cu12==0.8.0, and `pip index versions` on this machine returns "No matching distribution found" for both. Not a config problem; there is no macOS wheel in existence.
- Chai-1: README states "requires Linux, Python 3.10 or later, and a GPU with CUDA and bfloat16 support", and the source defaults to torch.device("cuda:0") with TorchScript modules exported for CUDA. TRAP WORTH FLAGGING: its PyPI metadata declares no CUDA dependencies, so `pip install chai_lab` will probably SUCCEED on macOS and then fail at runtime. Anyone who tests installability rather than execution will conclude it works. It does not.
- OmegaFold: last commit 2022-12-12, over three and a half years stale, 49 open issues, and no explicit weights-licence grant. Weights are still served (S3 returns HTTP 206) but do not build on it.
- AlphaFold 3 locally: Linux-only and CUDA CC 8.0+, so the licence question never even arises on this hardware.

THE ESM ATLAS FINDING — THE MOST IMPORTANT THING IN THIS AUDIT.
The fold API at api.esmatlas.com is ALIVE AT THE GATEWAY AND DEAD AT THE BACKEND, and it fails in the specific way that defeats a naive health check. Its validation layer is perfect and instant: 401 residues returns HTTP 413 "Sequence is longer than 400." (so the cap is EXACTLY 400, confirmed by bisecting the 400/401 boundary), empty body returns HTTP 400, bad characters return HTTP 422 with the full token set, GET returns HTTP 403. But actual inference never completes. I sent novel random sequences at lengths 10, 20, 30, 50, 80, 120 and 200 and every single one returned HTTP 504; a 30-mer failed 4 out of 4 times. The only HTTP 200 I ever obtained was for the trivial string MKTVRQERLK, returned in 0.105-0.326 s across three repeats — far too fast to be inference, i.e. a cached result from a previous user. If you smoke-test this endpoint with a common sequence you will get a 200 and conclude it works; every real user query will then 504. DO NOT BUILD ON IT. Also note that when it does serve a cached hit, the B-factor column carries PER-ATOM pLDDT ON A 0-1 SCALE (I observed 0.83/0.82/0.83/0.78/0.76 within a single residue), not the 0-100 AlphaFold convention — a parser assuming 0-100 will silently report every model as ~1% confident.

RECOMMENDED ARCHITECTURE.
Route by job type. Monomer, no ligand, speed matters: ESMFold local via transformers on MPS. Anything needing an MSA: api.colabfold.com for the alignment, then feed it onward. Complexes, ligands, or AF3-class accuracy: OpenFold3 or Boltz-2, hosted on NVIDIA if you have a key, local on MPS if you accept unvalidated throughput. Never silently downgrade between these — they emit different metrics on different scales.

PARSING — THE SCALE AND SEMANTICS TRAPS.
pLDDT is not one thing. AF3 = per-ATOM, 0-100. AF2/ColabFold/OpenFold = per-RESIDUE, 0-100. Boltz = per-TOKEN, 0-1. ESM Atlas API = per-ATOM, 0-1. OmegaFold = per-residue in the B-factor column. Normalise explicitly and assert the range at parse time; do not trust the source. Likewise the ranking scores are NOT interchangeable: AF3's ranking_score = 0.8 x ipTM + 0.2 x pTM + 0.5 x disorder - 100 x has_clash, range [-100, 1.5]; Boltz's confidence_score = 0.8 * complex_plddt + 0.2 * iptm (ptm for single chains), range [0,1]. Structurally parallel, different quantities — Boltz uses complex_plddt where AF3 uses ipTM, and carries no clash or disorder term. Never compare them numerically or sort a mixed list by "score". has_clash exists in AF3 and OpenFold3, has an analogue in Chai (has_inter_chain_clashes), and is ABSENT from Boltz — compute it yourself there rather than defaulting it to false.

WHAT CANNOT BE DONE WITHOUT AF3 WEIGHTS OR A GPU — STATE THESE PLAINLY.
1. You cannot run AlphaFold 3 itself. Not for licence reasons on this box but for OS reasons: it is Linux-only and needs CUDA CC 8.0+. Even with weights in hand it would not start on macOS.
2. You cannot obtain AF3 weights for a commercial product at all. They are non-commercial only, granted case-by-case, and only "if received directly from Google". If this platform is commercial, AF3 is permanently closed to it regardless of hardware.
3. You cannot train or distil anything on AF3 output. The terms explicitly forbid using AF3 output "to train machine learning models or related technology". This forecloses the obvious workaround.
4. You cannot redistribute AF3 weights, and you cannot legally consume a third-party mirror of them.
5. You cannot automate alphafoldserver.com. It is a web UI with a daily quota, a restricted ligand whitelist, and no documented REST API; scripting it would breach the terms.
6. You cannot reproduce exact AF3 numbers with any substitute. OpenFold3, Boltz-2, Chai-1 and Protenix are independent models, not reimplementations that reproduce AF3's values.
7. You should not promise local latency SLAs yet. I verified that OpenFold3 ships an official osx-arm64/MPS environment, but its own prerequisites section simultaneously says inference "requires a system with a GPU with a minimum of CUDA 12.1 and 32GB of memory" — the documentation contradicts itself, and the vendor publishes no Apple Silicon timing. Installation is supported; throughput and numerical fidelity on MPS are unvalidated. Measure before you advertise.
8. The honest disclosure line: whenever a request would have gone to AF3 and instead goes to OpenFold3, Boltz-2 or ESMFold, SAY SO IN THE OUTPUT, naming the model actually used and its confidence metric. Silent substitution of a weaker or merely different model is the failure mode to avoid.

OPEN ITEM I COULD NOT CLOSE. I confirmed the three NVIDIA routes are live by the 401-versus-404 method, and ruled out eight plausible-but-nonexistent paths, but I could NOT retrieve their request JSON schema, sequence-length caps or rate limits: build.nvidia.com pages timed out through the fetch tool and docs.nvidia.com/nim/bionemo/boltz-2/latest/api-reference.html returns HTTP 404. The model card at build.nvidia.com/mit/boltz2 does return HTTP 200, so the documentation exists — read it in a browser with an API key in hand before integrating. I have deliberately left those fields as "not retrieved" rather than guessing.

methods.name: AutoDock Vina scoring function (Vina SF)
methods.paper: Trott O, Olson AJ. "AutoDock Vina: improving the speed and accuracy of docking with a new scoring function, efficient optimization, and multithreading." J Comput Chem 2010;31:455-461. doi:10.1002/jcc.21334. Unchanged in Eberhardt J, Santos-Martins D, Tillack AF, Forli S. J Chem Inf Model 2021;61:3891-3898.
methods.equation:
Surface distance: d_ij = r_ij - R_ti - R_tj  (R_t = XS van der Waals radius of atom type t; r_ij = interatomic distance).

Total: c = SUM_{i<j} f_{ti,tj}(r_ij), split as c = c_inter + c_intra. Pairwise cutoff = 8 A.

Terms (all functions of d = d_ij):
  gauss1(d)      = exp( -(d/0.5 A)^2 )
  gauss2(d)      = exp( -((d - 3 A)/2 A)^2 )
  repulsion(d)   = d^2  if d < 0 ;  0  if d >= 0
  hydrophobic(d) = 1        if d < 0.5 A
                 = 0        if d > 1.5 A
                 = linear interpolation in between
                 (applied ONLY when both atoms are hydrophobic)
  HBond(d)       = 1        if d < -0.7 A
                 = 0        if d > 0
                 = linear interpolation in between
                 (applied ONLY when the pair is a donor/acceptor pair)

Reported affinity (paper Eq. 9, the conformation-independent function g):
  s = g(c_inter) = c_inter / (1 + w_rot * N_rot)
where N_rot = number of active rotatable bonds between heavy atoms in the ligand.

IMPORTANT: Eq. 9 is rendered as an IMAGE in the paper and is NOT machine-readable. The DIVISION form is confirmed from the reference implementation, src/lib/conf_independent.cpp, class num_tors_div:
   fl weight = 0.1 * (read_iterator(i) + 1);
   return conf_smooth_div(x, 1 + weight * in.num_tors / 5.0);
combined with src/lib/vina.cpp set_vina_weights, which stores (5 * weight_rot / 0.1 - 1). Substituting: weight = 5*w_rot, denominator = 1 + 5*w_rot*N_rot/5 = 1 + w_rot*N_rot. QED. Do NOT implement this as an addition -- an LLM summary of the PMC page returned the additive form and it is wrong.

Exact potential parameters from src/lib/scoring_function.h, case SF_VINA:
   vina_gaussian(offset=0,  width=0.5, cutoff=8.0)   -> gauss1
   vina_gaussian(offset=3,  width=2.0, cutoff=8.0)   -> gauss2
   vina_repulsion(offset=0.0,          cutoff=8.0)
   vina_hydrophobic(good=0.5, bad=1.5, cutoff=8.0)
   vina_non_dir_h_bond(good=-0.7, bad=0, cutoff=8.0)
   linearattraction(20.0)  [macrocycle 'glue' term, NOT part of the 2010 SF]
   num_tors_div()
methods.coefficients:
Table 1 of Trott & Olson 2010, transcribed verbatim from the PMC full text:
   -0.0356   gauss1
   -0.00516  gauss2
    0.840    repulsion
   -0.0351   hydrophobic
   -0.587    hydrogen bonding
    0.0585   N_rot

Full-precision values as shipped (src/lib/vina.h, set_vina_weights defaults) -- USE THESE:
   weight_gauss1      = -0.035579
   weight_gauss2      = -0.005156
   weight_repulsion   =  0.840245
   weight_hydrophobic = -0.035069
   weight_hydrogen    = -0.587439
   weight_glue        = 50        (macrocycle closure only)
   weight_rot         =  0.05846
Units: kcal/mol per unit of the corresponding term. The paper's rounded table and the source defaults agree to the printed precision.
inputs_required: 3D coordinates of receptor and ligand in PDBQT format (AutoDock atom types + Gasteiger charges, though Vina SF ignores charges)
XS atom typing (hydrophobic flag, H-bond donor/acceptor flag, per-type vdW radius R_t)
Count of active rotatable bonds N_rot in the ligand
Search box center and size (for docking; not needed for --score_only rescoring)
methods.reported_accuracy: Binding affinity: standard error 2.85 kcal/mol on the full test set; 2.75 kcal/mol on the 116 complexes not present in PDBbind. Quoted verbatim: "Vina achieves a comparatively low standard error of 2.85 kcal/mol" ... "The standard error for the 116 complexes not in PDBbind was 2.75 kcal/mol." Pose prediction (Vina 1.2.0 paper, DUD-E): top-1 success at <=2 A RMSD = 74%, top-2 = 80%, top-3 = 84%; at <=0.5 A only 28% top-1. Virtual screening on DUD-E: mean AUC 0.71 +/- 0.15, BEDROC(alpha=20) 0.26 +/- 0.19, EF(1%) 10.87 +/- 11.72. Note the 0.15 AUC standard deviation -- performance is strongly target-dependent, and for 17 of 50 DUD-E targets BEDROC < 0.1 (i.e. no useful enrichment).
methods.accuracy_dataset: Trott & Olson 2010: trained on the PDBbind refined set; affinity error reported on the AutoDock 4 test set of 190 protein-ligand X-ray complexes (116 of which are not in PDBbind). Eberhardt 2021: 50 targets from DUD-E, 4938 actives + 292,778 decoys, plus co-crystal redocking.
methods.applicability_domain: Small drug-like organic ligands in a well-defined, mostly buried pocket of a rigid protein. NOT valid for: metalloenzyme coordination (no explicit metal term), charged/highly polar ligands (the SF has NO electrostatics and NO desolvation term -- stated explicitly in the Vina 1.2.0 paper: "Vina lacks electrostatics and solvation"), covalent binders, very large or highly flexible ligands, and peptides (the N_rot divisor was fitted on drug-like N_rot ranges and degrades badly for the 20-60 rotatable bonds of a peptide). Do not use Vina SF for case (b) peptide/protein-protein.
methods.implementation_route: pip package name is `vina` (PyPI, currently 1.2.7). WARNING -- I attempted `pip install vina` on this machine and IT FAILED: `ValueError: Boost library location was not found!`. Cause verified against the PyPI JSON API: vina 1.2.7 ships wheels ONLY for manylinux/musllinux x86_64, cp38-cp312. There are NO macOS wheels for 1.2.7 at all (the last macOS wheels were 1.2.5, x86_64 only, cp36-cp39) and NO wheels for Python 3.13/3.14. On Apple Silicon + Python 3.14 pip falls back to an sdist build requiring Boost + SWIG. Working routes on this laptop: (1) `brew install boost swig` then pip install from sdist; (2) conda/mamba `conda install -c conda-forge vina`; (3) download the prebuilt `vina_1.2.5_mac_x86_64` binary and run under Rosetta 2; (4) reimplement the SF directly -- it is ~60 lines given XS typing, and the coefficients above are complete. Also available as the `--score_only` mode of the CLI for pure rescoring of an existing pose.

methods.paper: Quiroga R, Villarreal MA. "Vinardo: A scoring function based on AutoDock Vina improves scoring, docking, and virtual screening." PLoS One 2016;11:e0155183.
methods.paper_id: doi:10.1371/journal.pone.0155183 (paper NOT fetched; parameters taken from AutoDock-Vina source)
methods.equation:
Same architecture as Vina but a reduced term set, transcribed from src/lib/scoring_function.h, case SF_VINARDO:
   vinardo_gaussian(offset=0, width=0.8, cutoff=8.0)      -> single gaussian, NOT two
   vinardo_repulsion(offset=0,           cutoff=8.0)
   vinardo_hydrophobic(good=0, bad=2.5,  cutoff=8.0)
   vinardo_non_dir_h_bond(good=-0.6, bad=0, cutoff=8.0)
   num_tors_div()
Uses xs_vinardo_radius() (a different radius table from Vina) for optimal_distance. Same s = c_inter/(1 + w_rot*N_rot) form.
methods.coefficients: From src/lib/vina.h set_vinardo_weights defaults: weight_gauss1 = -0.045, weight_rot = 0.05846. NOTE: I retrieved only these two values from the header grep; the repulsion, hydrophobic and hydrogen weights were on source lines I did not capture. Commonly cited Vinardo values are repulsion 0.8, hydrophobic -0.035, hydrogen -0.600, but I did NOT verify these three against a fetched source, so treat them as UNVERIFIED and re-read src/lib/vina.h lines 127-130 before use.
inputs_required: Same as Vina (PDBQT, XS typing with Vinardo radii, N_rot)
methods.reported_accuracy: NOT RETRIEVED. I did not fetch the Quiroga & Villarreal 2016 paper; do not quote a number for Vinardo.
methods.accuracy_dataset: NOT RETRIEVED
methods.applicability_domain: Same as Vina; reported by its authors to improve scoring/ranking over Vina, but I have no verified figure to support that here.

methods.name: Smina
methods.paper: Koes DR, Baumgartner MP, Camacho CJ. "Lessons Learned in Empirical Scoring with smina from the CSAR 2011 Benchmarking Exercise." J Chem Inf Model 2013;53:1893-1904. doi:10.1021/ci300604z
methods.equation: Smina is a fork of AutoDock Vina, not a new scoring function. It ships the Vina SF (identical functional form and default weights as transcribed above) and exposes every term's weight as a user-editable text file (--custom_scoring), plus additional optional terms. The custom function developed in the paper is a reweighting of the Vina term set on CSAR 2010 data; I did NOT retrieve that custom weight vector, so only the default (= Vina) equation is transcribed here.
methods.coefficients: Default = the Vina weights above, verified identical. The paper's CSAR-2010-refitted custom weight vector: NOT RETRIEVED (paywalled at ACS; do not reconstruct).
inputs_required: Receptor + ligand (accepts PDB/PDBQT/SDF/MOL2 directly -- notably more forgiving than Vina, no PDBQT conversion needed)
Autobox from a reference ligand, or explicit box
methods.reported_accuracy: NOT RETRIEVED for the custom function. The paper's stated qualitative result is that the custom scoring function samples low-RMSD poses better than default Vina when cross-docking. Since smina's default SF is bit-identical to Vina's, the Vina accuracy figures (2.85 kcal/mol standard error) carry over for the default mode.
methods.accuracy_dataset: CSAR 2010 (training) / CSAR 2011 benchmarking exercise (evaluation)
methods.applicability_domain: Same as Vina. Practical advantage: fast rescoring mode (--score_only / --minimize) and native SDF I/O make it the most convenient way to apply the Vina SF to an existing pose.
methods.implementation_route: NOT on PyPI (verified: pypi.org/pypi/smina/json returns 404). Routes: `conda install -c conda-forge smina`, `brew install smina`, static Linux binary from SourceForge, or build from https://github.com/mwojcikowski/smina. Runs fine on a laptop CPU.

methods.name: gnina (CNN-rescored docking)
methods.paper: McNutt AT, Francoeur P, Aggarwal R, Masuda T, Meli R, Ragoza M, Sunseri J, Koes DR. "GNINA 1.0: molecular docking with deep learning." J Cheminform 2021;13:43. And McNutt AT, Li Y, Meli R, Aggarwal R, Koes DR. "GNINA 1.3: the next increment in molecular docking with deep learning." J Cheminform 2025.
methods.equation: EQUATION NOT RETRIEVED -- none exists in closed form. gnina uses the Vina/Vinardo SF for sampling, then rescores poses with an ensemble of 3D convolutional neural networks operating on a voxelized atomic-density grid of the binding site. The CNN has two output heads: (i) CNNscore, a pose-quality/binder probability in [0,1], and (ii) CNNaffinity, trained with MSE loss against pK (pKd/pKi). Weights are learned network parameters, not publishable coefficients.
methods.coefficients: N/A -- neural network weights. Distributed as model checkpoint files with the software.
inputs_required: Binding site box, typically via --autobox_ligand from a reference ligand
methods.reported_accuracy: GNINA 1.3, verified from the PMC full text: redocking on the PoseBusters benchmark 67% top-1 success; cross-docking on the Wierbowski set, top-1 improved from 37% to 40% with the default ensemble. CRITICAL: the GNINA 1.3 paper does NOT report Pearson r or RMSE for the CNNaffinity output. Do not quote an affinity accuracy for gnina from this paper. GNINA 1.0 reported that CNN rescoring outperforms Vina scoring on redocking/cross-docking pose selection -- again a POSE metric, not an affinity metric.
methods.accuracy_dataset: PoseBusters benchmark (redocking); Wierbowski cross-docking set; PDBbind core set v2016 (100-complex subset, used for the runtime benchmark)
methods.applicability_domain: Small molecules only. CNN scoring functions are known to be sensitive to train/test leakage and to generalize poorly to protein families absent from CrossDocked2020 training data. CNNaffinity is a pK regression, so it is at least dimensionally an affinity -- unlike CNNscore, which is a pose-quality probability and must never be reported as an affinity.
methods.implementation_route: NOT on PyPI (verified: 404). Officially Linux-only with a Docker container; build from https://github.com/gnina/gnina. Runs CPU-only (no GPU required) -- the 1.3 paper measures ~23 s per complex on 4 CPU cores for the default ensemble and ~16 s for the 'fast' model, on the PDBbind core v2016 subset. On macOS, Docker is the practical route.

methods.name: RF-Score (Random Forest rescoring)
methods.paper: Ballester PJ, Mitchell JBO. "A machine learning approach to predicting protein-ligand binding affinity with applications to molecular docking." Bioinformatics 2010;26(9):1169-1175.
methods.equation:
No closed form -- a Random Forest regression. The FEATURES are exactly specified and are the fully reproducible part:
  x_{j,i} = number of occurrences of protein atom type j paired with ligand atom type i within a cutoff distance d_cutoff.
Element types used for BOTH protein and ligand: C, N, O, F, P, S, Cl, Br, I (9 types) -> 81 candidate pairs, of which 45 are always zero (those elements absent from proteinogenic residues), leaving 36 non-zero features. d_cutoff = 12 A, chosen as "sufficiently large to implicitly capture solvation effects". Target variable is pKd/pKi. The trained forest itself is the model; there are no publishable coefficients. Marked equation_retrieved=true because the complete, reproducible feature specification was retrieved -- the model is non-parametric by construction.
methods.coefficients: N/A -- Random Forest (500 trees in the original). The reproducible specification is the 36-element-pair feature definition with a 12 A cutoff, given above.
inputs_required: A 3D pose of the protein-ligand complex (crystal or docked)
Element identity of every protein and ligand heavy atom within 12 A
A trained RF model (retrain on PDBbind, or use the ODDT-bundled pretrained models)
methods.reported_accuracy: Pearson Rp = 0.776, Spearman Rs = 0.762, RMSE = 1.58 in log Kd/Ki units (NOT kcal/mol -- multiply by 1.364 for kcal/mol at 298 K, giving ~2.16 kcal/mol).
methods.accuracy_dataset: Trained on the PDBbind v2007 refined set minus the core set = 1,105 complexes; tested on the PDBbind v2007 core set = 195 diverse complexes. This is the classic benchmark; note the well-documented caveat that PDBbind core-set performance is inflated by protein-family overlap between train and test.
methods.applicability_domain: Small molecules with elements in {C,N,O,F,P,S,Cl,Br,I}. Silently ignores metals, boron, silicon, and any other element -- a complex with a critical Zn or B contact will be scored as if that atom did not exist. Strongly biased toward protein families well represented in PDBbind; generalization to novel targets is substantially worse than the 0.776 headline suggests.
methods.implementation_route: pip install oddt (Open Drug Discovery Toolkit, PyPI 0.7 -- verified present on PyPI). ODDT reimplements RF-Score (v1/v2/v3), NNScore and PLECscore with pretrained models and an `oddt.scoring` API. ODDT needs RDKit or OpenBabel as a backend; RDKit 2026.3.5 is already in the project venv at /Users/seunghojung/Documents/DeepMind_Bio/.venv/bin/python. Alternatively retrain from scratch with scikit-learn -- the feature definition above is complete and takes ~30 lines. Scoring is milliseconds per complex on a laptop CPU. NOTE: I verified oddt is on PyPI but did NOT install and run it, unlike prodigy/openmm which I did execute.

methods.name: NNScore 2.0 (neural network rescoring)
methods.paper: Durrant JD, McCammon JA. "NNScore 2.0: A Neural-Network Receptor-Ligand Scoring Function." J Chem Inf Model 2011;51(11):2897-2903. doi:10.1021/ci2003889

Output is an estimate of pKd. There is no closed-form equation and I did not retrieve the network weights. Do not reconstruct.
methods.coefficients: N/A -- 20 network weight matrices, distributed with the software. Not retrieved.
inputs_required: A Vina executable (NNScore 2.0 calls Vina to generate its Vina-term inputs)
methods.reported_accuracy: NOT RELIABLY RETRIEVED. The primary NNScore 2.0 paper is paywalled and is principally a VIRTUAL SCREENING / enrichment paper, not an affinity-regression paper. A secondary comparison surfaced Pearson 0.629 +/- 0.002 and RMSE 1.391 +/- 0.004, but I could NOT trace this to the primary paper and could not identify which dataset it refers to. DO NOT quote these numbers. Treat NNScore 2.0 as having no verified affinity accuracy for this platform's purposes.
methods.accuracy_dataset: NOT RETRIEVED

methods.name: PRODIGY (IC-NIS model) -- protein-protein and peptide-protein
methods.paper: Vangone A, Bonvin AMJJ. "Contacts-based prediction of binding affinity in protein-protein complexes." eLife 2015;4:e07454. doi:10.7554/eLife.07454. Web server: Xue LC, Rodrigues JP, Kastritis PL, Bonvin AMJJ, Vangone A. "PRODIGY: a web server for predicting the binding affinity of protein-protein complexes." Bioinformatics 2016;32(23):3676-3678.
methods.equation:
Equation (2) of Vangone & Bonvin 2015, extracted VERBATIM from the eLife JATS XML MathML node (disp-formula id="equ2"):

  dGcalc = 0.09459*ICs_charged/charged + 0.10007*ICs_charged_apolar - 0.19577*ICs_polar/polar + 0.22671*ICs_polar/apolar - 0.18681*%NIS_apolar - 0.13810*%NIS_charged + 15.9433

*** CRITICAL SIGN WARNING -- READ BEFORE IMPLEMENTING ***
Equation 2 AS PRINTED returns a POSITIVE number and is NOT a binding free energy. The shipping reference implementation (prodigy_prot/modules/models.py, function IC_NIS) negates EVERY term:

  dG = -0.09459*ic_cc - 0.10007*ic_ca + 0.19577*ic_pp - 0.22671*ic_pa + 0.18681*p_nis_a + 0.13810*p_nis_c - 15.9433

I verified this numerically. Running the installed tool on 1YCR (MDM2 chain A + p53 peptide chain B) gives ic_cc=5, ic_ca=11, ic_pp=4, ic_pa=7, %NIS_apolar=31.51, %NIS_charged=34.25. Equation 2 as printed evaluates to +7.705; the negated form evaluates to -7.705, which is exactly what the tool prints (-7.7 kcal/mol). USE THE NEGATED FORM.

Term definitions:
  ICs_xx = COUNT of inter-residue contacts across the interface of the given polarity class, where a contact exists if ANY heavy atom of a residue in partner 1 is within 5.5 A of ANY heavy atom of a residue in partner 2 (re-optimized cutoff; the paper first used 4.0 A and moved to 5.5 A).
  %NIS_x = PERCENTAGE (0-100, not a fraction) of residues of class x on the NON-interacting surface, i.e. solvent-accessible residues NOT part of the interface. Computed with freesasa.
  Residue polarity classes (prodigy_prot/modules/aa_properties.py, aa_character_ic):
    Apolar (A): ALA CYS GLY PHE ILE MET LEU PRO TRP VAL TYR
    Charged (C): GLU ASP HIS LYS ARG      <- note HIS is CHARGED in this classification
    Polar (P): ASN GLN SER THR
  NOTE: ICs_charged/polar and ICs_apolar/apolar are computed and printed by the tool but are NOT in the model -- AIC stepwise selection dropped them. Do not include them.

Kd conversion (prodigy_prot/modules/utils.py, dg_to_kd):
  Kd = exp( dG / (R*T) ), R = 0.0019858775 kcal/mol/K, T = temperature_C + 273.15 (default 25 C).
methods.coefficients:
As transcribed above. Intercept = 15.9433 (printed) / -15.9433 (as implemented). Contact cutoff 5.5 A.

DISCREPANCY TO BE AWARE OF: Table 3 of the same paper (Model 6) lists slightly DIFFERENT magnitudes for the same model: ICs_cc 0.09420, ICs_ca 0.10038, ICs_pp -0.19522, ICs_pa 0.22609, %NIS_apolar -0.18786, %NIS_charged -0.13872, intercept 15.9433. The intercept matches but the six slopes differ in the 3rd-4th decimal. Equation 2 -- not Table 3 -- is what the released software implements, and Equation 2 is what I verified reproduces the tool's output exactly. Use Equation 2's magnitudes with negated signs.
inputs_required: A 3D structure of the COMPLEX (PDB or mmCIF) -- this is a rescoring method, it cannot predict affinity from sequence and cannot dock
Chain identifiers for the two interacting partners
Nothing else: no charges, no force field, no minimization, no MD
methods.reported_accuracy: Pearson R = -0.73 (p < 0.0001) between predicted and experimental binding affinity, RMSE = 1.89 kcal/mol. (The R is reported as negative in Table 3 because of the paper's sign convention; the magnitude 0.73 is what the authors and the 2019 follow-up quote, e.g. "a Pearson's Correlation coefficient of 0.73 ... and root mean square error (RMSE) of 1.89 kcal/mol".) For context, the same paper's Table 3 shows the simpler nested models reach only R = -0.46 to -0.67.
methods.accuracy_dataset: The 'cleaned' dataset: 81 protein-protein complexes, a curated subset of the Kastritis et al. (2011) structure-based protein-protein binding affinity benchmark (originally 144/122 complexes), reduced to 81 by removing affinities measured by unreliable methods (inhibition assays, fluorescence spectrophotometry, potentiometry, radioligand, reduction assay, sedimentation) and incomplete structures. Later validated against the Vreven et al. (2015) affinity benchmark v2.
methods.applicability_domain: *** THIS IS THE MOST IMPORTANT CAVEAT FOR THE PEPTIDE USE CASE. *** The training set is 81 GLOBULAR PROTEIN-PROTEIN complexes. It contains NO short peptides. Both model terms are problematic for peptides: (a) %NIS is defined over the non-interacting surface, but for a 10-15 residue peptide essentially the ENTIRE peptide is interface, so its NIS contribution is near-meaningless and the %NIS values end up dominated entirely by the large partner; (b) the model has no term for the large conformational-entropy penalty a disordered peptide pays on binding, which is often the dominant term for peptide binding. Empirically it still lands in the right ballpark -- I measured -7.7 kcal/mol for MDM2/p53 (experimental ~-8.5 to -8.9 kcal/mol, Kd ~300-700 nM) and -11.6 kcal/mol for TEM1/BLIP (1JTG, experimental ~-13.7 kcal/mol, Kd ~0.1 nM) -- but both are ~1-2 kcal/mol underbound, consistent with the stated 1.89 kcal/mol RMSE and NOT better than it. Report peptide predictions as off-domain with an error bar of at least +/-1.9 kcal/mol, preferably wider. Also: the method is deterministic given a structure, so it inherits 100% of the error in a predicted (AlphaFold/docked) complex -- it has no way to know the pose is wrong.
methods.implementation_route: pip install prodigy-prot (PyPI 2.4.0). VERIFIED WORKING ON THIS MACHINE: installed cleanly into a Python 3.14 venv with only pure-Python/wheel deps (biopython 1.88, freesasa 2.2.1, numpy 2.5.2). CLI: `prodigy complex.pdb --selection A B`. Measured runtime on Apple M5 Max: 0.44 s for 1JTG (TEM1/BLIP, ~470 residues), ~2.0 s for 1YCR including interpreter startup. Also importable as a library (prodigy_prot.modules.models.IC_NIS). This is BY FAR the best option for case (b) on a laptop. GOTCHA I HIT LIVE: for a PDB with multiple copies in the asymmetric unit you must select the correct BIOLOGICAL pair -- selecting A,B vs C,D on 1JTG scored a crystal contact and returned -7.0 kcal/mol instead of the correct -11.6 kcal/mol, with no warning. Validate chain selection against the biological assembly.

methods.name: PRODIGY simple single-property estimators (contact-count and buried-surface-area)
methods.paper: Vangone A, Bonvin AMJJ, eLife 2015;4:e07454, Table 3, Models 1-5, and Equation 3 for BSA.
methods.equation:
These are the published simple contact-based and BSA-based empirical estimators, transcribed from Table 3 of the same paper. General form dG_calc = w1*P1 + ... + Q.

Model 1 (contact count only):    dG_calc = 0.07782 * ICs_total + 4.78839
Model 2 (buried surface area):   dG_calc = 0.00278 * BSA_total + 5.66032
Model 3 (contact types, no NIS): dG_calc = 0.11627*ICs_charged/apolar - 0.12655*ICs_polar/polar + 0.23595*ICs_polar/apolar + 5.13766
Model 4 (hydrophobic classes):   dG_calc = 0.09055*ICs_hydrophil/hydrophil + 0.05726*ICs_hydrophil/hydrophob + 0.06037*ICs_hydrophob/hydrophil + 4.90452
Model 5 (polar/apolar BSA):      dG_calc = 0.00131*BSA_polar + 0.00400*BSA_apolar + 5.44809

SAME SIGN CAVEAT AS THE MAIN MODEL: as printed these return positive numbers. Negate to obtain a binding free energy.

BSA (paper Eq. 3) = (ASA_protein1 + ASA_protein2) - ASA_complex, in A^2. ICs use the 5.5 A heavy-atom cutoff.
methods.coefficients: As above, verbatim from Table 3 of the eLife XML.
inputs_required: A solvent-accessible-surface-area calculator (freesasa) for the BSA models
methods.reported_accuracy:
Model 1 (ICs_total):  R = -0.59, p < 0.0001, RMSE = 2.25 kcal/mol
Model 2 (BSA_total):  R = -0.46, p < 0.0001, RMSE = 2.46 kcal/mol
Model 3:              R = -0.67, p < 0.0001, RMSE = 2.08 kcal/mol
Model 4:              R = -0.60, p < 0.0001, RMSE = 2.22 kcal/mol
Model 5:              R = -0.48, p < 0.0001, RMSE = 2.45 kcal/mol
(Full IC-NIS model 6 for comparison: R = -0.73, RMSE = 1.89 kcal/mol)

Single-property Pearson correlations against experimental dG on the same 81-complex set (Table 2): ICs_total -0.59, BSA_total -0.46, BSA_apolar -0.47, BSA_polar -0.36, ICs_polar/apolar -0.56, ICs_hydrophilic/hydrophilic -0.53, ICs_charged/apolar -0.45, ICs_apolar/apolar -0.34, ICs_hydrophilic/hydrophobic -0.34, %NIS_apolar -0.33, %NIS_charged +0.28, ICs_charged/polar -0.26, ICs_charged/charged -0.17 (p=0.06, NOT significant alone), ICs_polar/polar -0.13 (p=0.1, NOT significant alone), ICs_hydrophobic/hydrophilic -0.05 (p=0.3, not significant).
methods.accuracy_dataset: Same 81-complex 'cleaned' subset of the Kastritis protein-protein affinity benchmark.
methods.applicability_domain: THE REAL LIMIT, stated numerically: a pure buried-surface-area estimator explains only R^2 = 0.21 of the variance in binding affinity (R = -0.46), and a pure contact count only R^2 = 0.35. An RMSE of 2.25-2.46 kcal/mol is a factor of ~40-60x in Kd. These are order-of-magnitude sanity checks, not measurements. They are useful only to bracket a prediction or to flag an outlier, never to rank close analogues. Note also that BSA correlates with affinity largely because both correlate with complex size -- it carries almost no information about interaction QUALITY, so it cannot distinguish a good interface from a large bad one.
methods.implementation_route: Trivial to implement directly: ~40 lines with Biopython (NeighborSearch for the 5.5 A residue contacts) and freesasa (for BSA/NIS). Both are pip-installable and both are already present as prodigy-prot dependencies (verified installed: biopython 1.88, freesasa 2.2.1). Sub-second per complex.

methods.name: PRODIGY-LIG (protein-small ligand)
methods.paper: Vangone A, Schaarschmidt J, Koukos P, Geng C, Citro N, Trellet ME, Xue LC, Bonvin AMJJ. "Large-scale prediction of binding affinity in protein-small ligand complexes: the PRODIGY-LIG web server." Bioinformatics 2019;35(9):1585-1587. doi:10.1093/bioinformatics/bty816. Underlying model: Kurkcuoglu Z, et al. J Comput Aided Mol Des 2018;32:175-185.
methods.equation:
Three published models, transcribed from the Bioinformatics 2019 paper (Eqs. 1-3), cross-checked against src/prodigy_lig/prodigy_lig.py.

Eq. 1 -- dG_score (for RANKING ligands; note the +187 intercept, this is not an energy):
  dG_score = 0.343794*E_elec - 0.037597*AC_CC + 0.138738*AC_NN + 0.160043*AC_OO - 3.088861*AC_XX + 187.011384

Eq. 2 -- dG_prediction, WITH electrostatics:
  dG = 0.0115148*E_elec - 0.0014852*AC_CC + 0.0057097*AC_NN - 0.1301806*AC_XX - 5.1002233

Eq. 3 -- dG_prediction, NO electrostatics (the only one usable without HADDOCK):
  dG = 0.0354707*AC_NN - 0.1277895*AC_XX - 0.0072166*AC_CN - 5.1923181

AC_xy = count of intermolecular ATOMIC contacts between protein and ligand within a 10.5 A cutoff, classified by element: C=carbon, N=nitrogen, O=oxygen, X=all other atoms and polar hydrogens. E_elec = intermolecular electrostatic energy from a HADDOCK refinement.

DISCREPANCY FLAGGED: the PDF text of Eq. 3 renders the -0.1277895 term as AC_CC, but the reference implementation (calculate_DG) applies it to contact_counts["XX"], and Eqs. 1 and 2 both attach a large-magnitude negative coefficient to AC_XX (-3.089 and -0.130). I judge the PDF to contain a typo (or my PDF extraction mangled the subscript) and the code to be correct. I have written AC_XX above, matching the code. Verify against the code, not the PDF.
methods.coefficients: As transcribed. Contact cutoff 10.5 A (verified in source: `def __init__(self, structure, chains, electrostatics, cutoff=10.5)` and `def calc_atomic_contacts(structure, chains, cutoff=10.5)`).
inputs_required: Protein chain ID, and the ligand chain + 3-letter residue name (syntax: -c A A:BTN)
For Eqs. 1-2 only: the HADDOCK intermolecular electrostatic energy -- which requires running HADDOCK, so in practice use Eq. 3
methods.reported_accuracy:
D3R Grand Challenge 2 Stage 2, blind, 102 protein-ligand complexes: Kendall's tau = 0.37 using docked models (ranked 9th of 82+ submissions); tau = 0.43 had the crystal structures been used (would have ranked 3rd).
PDBbind core_set_v2013, 124 entries with experimentally determined Ki: Pearson r = 0.57, p < 0.0001, RMSE = 2.6 kcal/mol ('no electrostatic protocol', i.e. Eq. 3).
methods.accuracy_dataset: Trained on 200 protein-small-ligand complexes from the 2P2I database (interfaces refined with HADDOCK). Tested blind on D3R Grand Challenge 2 Stage 2 (102 complexes) and independently on PDBbind core set v2013 (124 entries with Ki).
methods.applicability_domain: RMSE 2.6 kcal/mol is WORSE than Vina's 2.85 is good -- this is a coarse estimator. A Kendall tau of 0.37-0.43 means it gets roughly 70% of pairwise rankings right, i.e. it is a triage tool. I ran it on 1STP (streptavidin + biotin) and got -7.15 kcal/mol against an experimental ~-18 kcal/mol (Kd ~1e-14 M) -- an 11 kcal/mol error. Biotin-streptavidin is the canonical extreme outlier, but this is exactly why the method must never be presented as quantitative: a simple atomic-contact count has no way to represent an exceptionally preorganized, hydrogen-bond-saturated site. Its real strength is that it is generic and needs no atom typing, charges or parameterization.
methods.implementation_route: pip install prodigy-lig (PyPI 1.1.4). VERIFIED WORKING ON THIS MACHINE. CLI: `prodigy_lig -c A A:BTN -i 1STP.pdb`. Measured runtime 0.24 s. Chain/ligand spec must be uppercase and colon-separated or it raises RuntimeError. Only Eq. 3 is usable without a HADDOCK run.

methods.name: MM-GBSA / MM-PBSA (endpoint free energy)
methods.paper: Genheden S, Ryde U. "The MM/PBSA and MM/GBSA methods to estimate ligand-binding affinities." Expert Opin Drug Discov 2015;10(5):449-461. Benchmarks: Hou T, et al. J Chem Inf Model 2011;51:69-82 (part 1, small molecules); Chen F, et al. 2016 (part 6, protein-protein); part 10 (2019).
methods.equation:
dG_bind = <G_complex> - <G_protein> - <G_ligand>, each averaged over MD snapshots, with

  G = E_bonded + E_electrostatic + E_vdW + G_polar-solvation + G_nonpolar-solvation - T*S

  G_polar    = solved by Poisson-Boltzmann (MM/PBSA) or by a Generalized Born model (MM/GBSA)
  G_nonpolar = gamma * SASA + b   (the standard LCPO surface-area term)
  -T*S       = conformational entropy, usually from normal-mode or quasi-harmonic analysis

In the near-universal 'single-trajectory' protocol, snapshots for all three states are taken from one simulation of the complex, so E_bonded cancels exactly. The entropy term is very commonly OMITTED entirely, in which case the quantity computed is an ENTHALPY-LIKE INTERACTION ENERGY and must not be called a free energy.

This is a protocol, not a single equation with universal coefficients -- the numbers depend on the force field, the GB model (HCT/OBC1/OBC2/GBn/GBn2), the interior dielectric constant, and the salt concentration. There is no canonical coefficient set to transcribe, which is itself the honest finding.
methods.coefficients: No universal published coefficients. The tunable parameters that dominate the answer: solute interior dielectric (1, 2, or 4 -- Hou et al. found predictions are 'quite sensitive' to this and that it must be chosen per interface), GB model choice, and gamma/b in the nonpolar term. Hou et al. 2011 found the Onufriev-Case GB model (OBC) best for ranking. Chen et al. 2016 recommend eps_in = 1 for MM/GBSA and a higher value for MM/PBSA.
inputs_required: Parameterized topology: a protein force field (e.g. amber14SB) AND ligand parameters (GAFF2 + AM1-BCC charges, which requires antechamber/openff -- this is the real bottleneck for a novel small molecule)
An MD trajectory (typically 5-50 ns) of the complex, or at minimum a set of minimized snapshots
Optionally a normal-mode entropy calculation (very expensive; usually skipped)
methods.reported_accuracy:
Small molecules (Hou et al. 2011, part 1): the honest summary is that MM/PBSA is better for ABSOLUTE binding free energies while MM/GBSA is better for RANKING; predictions vary strongly with MD length (longer is NOT always better), dielectric constant, and snapshot count.
Protein-protein (Chen et al., part 6, 2016): best MM/GBSA setup (ff02, Onufriev GB, eps_in=1) gives Pearson rp = -0.647 on 46 protein-protein complexes; MM/PBSA gives rp = -0.523; empirical protein-protein docking scoring functions on the same set span rp = -0.141 to -0.529.
Part 10 (2019): standard MM/GBSA from conventional MD gives rp = -0.523 on 21 protein-protein complexes vs MM/PBSA rp = -0.212; accelerated-MD (aMD/GaMD) sampling did NOT improve things.
Genheden & Ryde's expert opinion is deliberately deflationary: the methods "contain several crude and questionable approximations, for example, the lack of conformational entropy and information about the number and free energy of water molecules in the binding site", "their performance varies strongly with the tested system", and "most attempts to ameliorate the methods with more accurate approaches, for example, quantum-mechanical calculations, polarizable force fields or improved solvation have deteriorated the results". They also report that independent MM/PBSA calculations of the SAME system can differ by more than 10 kcal/mol for small-molecule complexes -- i.e. the run-to-run precision can be worse than the entire dynamic range of interest.
methods.accuracy_dataset: Hou 2011 part 1: 59 ligands across 6 proteins. Chen 2016 part 6: 46 protein-protein complexes (+43 for pose re-ranking against ZDOCK decoys). Part 10 2019: 21 protein-protein complexes.
methods.applicability_domain: Best used for RELATIVE ranking within a congeneric series against a single target, with a fixed protocol. Not trustworthy for absolute affinities. Known to fail on: interfaces with buried structural waters, large charge changes between ligands (the GB polar term is very sensitive to net charge), significant conformational reorganization on binding, and anything where entropy dominates -- which includes most peptide binding.
methods.implementation_route:
A pure-pip Python route EXISTS and I VERIFIED IT ON THIS MACHINE: `pip install openmm pdbfixer` installed cleanly (openmm 8.5.2, pdbfixer 1.12.0) into a Python 3.14 venv. Platforms exposed: Reference, CPU, OpenCL. Implicit-solvent GB models available in openmm.app: HCT, OBC1, OBC2, GBn, GBn2 (load via ForceField('amber14-all.xml','implicit/obc2.xml')).

REAL MEASURED RUNTIME (Apple M5 Max, 18 cores, OpenMM CPU platform, 1670-atom system = MDM2 + p53 peptide from 1YCR, amber14SB + OBC2 implicit solvent, 2 fs timestep, H-bond constraints, 2 nm cutoff): 2000 steps (4 ps) in 30.2 s = 11.4 ns/day. So 1 ns takes 2.1 hours. A minimal 5 ns MM-GBSA production run on this SMALL system is ~10.5 hours of laptop CPU. A realistic drug target (3-5x more atoms) drops to roughly 2-4 ns/day, i.e. multiple days per complex. CONCLUSION: MM-GBSA is technically laptop-runnable but is NOT interactive and does not scale past a handful of complexes. Note also that OpenMM alone does not solve ligand parameterization -- you still need GAFF/openff-toolkit for a novel small molecule, a separate and often painful dependency. For peptides (standard residues only) no extra parameterization is needed, which makes the peptide case considerably easier than the small-molecule case here.

methods.name: Alchemical free energy perturbation (FEP / TI) -- OUT OF SCOPE ON A LAPTOP
methods.paper: Wang L, Wu Y, Deng Y, Abel R, et al. "Accurate and reliable prediction of relative ligand binding potency in prospective drug discovery by way of a modern free-energy calculation protocol and force field." J Am Chem Soc 2015;137(7):2695-2703. doi:10.1021/ja512751q. Follow-up: Abel R, et al. Acc Chem Res 2017;50:1625-1632.
methods.equation:
Zwanzig free energy perturbation:
  dG(A->B) = -k_B*T * ln < exp( -(H_B - H_A)/(k_B*T) ) >_A
Evaluated over a series of intermediate lambda windows coupling the two end states, with the ensemble average taken from equilibrium MD at each window. Free energy differences are combined with BAR/MBAR estimators. Relative binding free energy uses the thermodynamic cycle:
  ddG_bind(A->B) = dG_transform(A->B, bound) - dG_transform(A->B, solvated)
There are no fitted coefficients -- this is a statistical-mechanically rigorous identity. Its accuracy is limited by force field quality and by sampling convergence, not by a regression fit.
methods.coefficients: None -- no empirical coefficients. Accuracy is bounded by the underlying force field (e.g. OPLS3/OPLS4, Amber, CHARMM) and by sampling convergence.
inputs_required: A high-quality bound pose (FEP does not fix a wrong pose -- it amplifies it)
Full explicit-solvent system: complex, ligand in water, ions, periodic box
Validated force field parameters for BOTH ligands, including a matched atom mapping between the perturbation endpoints
12-24 lambda windows per transformation, each requiring nanoseconds of equilibrium MD, typically with replica exchange (FEP/REST)
methods.reported_accuracy: Wang et al. 2015: RMSE 1.1 kcal/mol across 200 ligands and 10 targets. Abel et al. 2017 (aggregated across real prospective drug-discovery projects): average RMSE 1.1 kcal/mol, median RMSE 1.0 kcal/mol, average R^2 0.57, median R^2 0.57. NOTE: 1.1 kcal/mol is roughly a 6x error in Kd -- FEP is the most accurate practical method and it is still not better than that. Anything claiming better than ~1 kcal/mol should be disbelieved. (The 1.1 kcal/mol figure was corroborated across four independent sources; the JACS abstract itself does not state it, and I could not extract the Acc Chem Res PDF text directly, so treat it as well-corroborated rather than transcribed from a primary full text.)
methods.accuracy_dataset: Wang et al. 2015: 200 ligands across 10 protein targets (retrospective), plus prospective application in live projects. Abel et al. 2017: aggregate across internal Schrodinger project deployments.
methods.applicability_domain: RELATIVE binding free energies within a congeneric series -- ligands differing by small, alchemically mappable chemical changes on a common scaffold. It cannot compare scaffolds that are not mappable, and absolute FEP is far harder and less reliable. Requires a correct, stable binding pose as input.
methods.implementation_route: *** OUT OF SCOPE ON A LAPTOP CPU. DO NOT ATTEMPT. *** Concrete arithmetic from my own measurement: I measured 11.4 ns/day on this Apple M5 Max (18 CPU cores) for a 1,670-atom IMPLICIT-solvent system. An FEP calculation needs EXPLICIT solvent, which for a typical protein-ligand box is 30,000-50,000 atoms -- roughly 20-30x more atoms and with PME electrostatics, so realistically ~0.3-0.5 ns/day on this CPU. A single relative transformation needs ~12-24 lambda windows x ~5 ns each x 2 legs (bound + solvated) = roughly 120-240 ns of sampling. At 0.4 ns/day that is 300-600 DAYS of laptop CPU time FOR ONE LIGAND PAIR. On a modern GPU the same calculation is ~2-6 hours. This is a 3-4 order-of-magnitude gap and it is not closable by optimization. Open-source stacks exist (OpenFE / openmmtools / perses / GROMACS+PMX) and are worth using -- on a GPU cluster, not here. Consistent with this, Boltz-2 markets itself as "over 1000 times faster" than FEP.

methods.name: Boltz-2 binding affinity prediction head
methods.paper: Passaro S, Corso G, et al. "Boltz-2: Towards Accurate and Efficient Binding Affinity Prediction." 2025 (MIT / Recursion).
methods.equation:
EQUATION NOT RETRIEVED -- none exists in closed form. Boltz-2's affinity module is a deep neural network head attached to a structure-prediction trunk. It takes the co-folded protein-ligand complex representation and emits two outputs:
  (1) a continuous regression value standardized to log10 of concentration in MICROMOLAR units, approximately interpretable as an IC50-like value. The paper is explicit that this is trained on MIXED biochemical endpoints (Ki, Kd, IC50, AC50, EC50, XC50) all converted to that single scale.
  (2) a binary binding-likelihood classification.
Weights are distributed as model checkpoints, not coefficients.
methods.coefficients: N/A -- learned network parameters.
inputs_required: Protein sequence (and MSA, depending on configuration)
methods.reported_accuracy:
FEP+ benchmark (4-target subset): Pearson r = 0.66. The paper claims this "approaches state-of-the-art free energy simulations" while being "over 1000 times faster".
CASP16 affinity challenge: 140 protein-ligand pairs, blind; reported to outperform all top-ranking participants by a clear margin.
MF-PCBA virtual screening: enrichment factor 18.4 at the 0.5% threshold, roughly doubling the average precision of prior ML approaches.
Internal Recursion assays: Pearson r > 0.55 on only 3 of 8 assays -- performance is variable, and this is the most honest number in the paper for real prospective use.
The paper does NOT report a per-prediction runtime or GPU specification.
methods.accuracy_dataset: FEP+ benchmark (4-target subset); CASP16 affinity challenge (140 protein-ligand pairs); MF-PCBA; 8 internal Recursion assays.
methods.applicability_domain: Small molecules only -- the affinity head is a protein-SMALL MOLECULE model and does not address the peptide/protein-protein case at all. Because it is trained on pooled Ki/Kd/IC50/EC50, its output is NOT a thermodynamic binding constant: IC50 is assay- and substrate-concentration-dependent, so the target variable itself is not a single physical quantity. Independent evaluations already exist and are more sober than the paper (e.g. "On the Reliability of AI Methods in Drug Discovery: Evaluation of Boltz-2" (arxiv:2603.05532 / PMC13472093), which reports significant global RMSD variation in Boltz-2 structures versus docking, and "Assessing Boltz-2 Performance for the Binding Classification of Docking Hits" (PMID 41592323)) -- consult these before deploying.
methods.implementation_route: pip install boltz. NOT PRACTICAL ON A LAPTOP CPU: Boltz-2 is a large co-folding transformer requiring a CUDA GPU with substantial VRAM for usable throughput; CPU inference is possible in principle but takes many minutes to hours per complex and needs large RAM. I confirmed this machine exposes only Reference/CPU/OpenCL compute platforms (no CUDA). Treat as a cloud/GPU-only option, out of scope for the stated laptop-CPU requirement.

methods.name: Ligand efficiency and the maximal-affinity ceiling (sanity-check layer)
methods.paper: Kuntz ID, Chen K, Sharp KA, Kollman PA. "The maximal affinity of ligands." Proc Natl Acad Sci USA 1999;96(18):9997-10002. And Hopkins AL, Groom CR, Alex A. "Ligand efficiency: a useful metric for lead selection." Drug Discov Today 2004;9(10):430-431.
methods.equation:
Ligand efficiency (Hopkins, Groom & Alex 2004):
  LE = -dG_bind / N_heavy
with dG in kcal/mol and N_heavy = HAC = heavy (non-hydrogen) atom count. Equivalently LE ~= 1.364 * pKd / HAC at 298 K.

Kuntz et al. 1999 maximal-affinity relation: binding free energy rises with the number of non-hydrogen atoms with an initial slope of approximately -1.5 kcal/mol per atom, then PLATEAUS at ~15 heavy atoms, beyond which affinity increases very little with added mass. The observed ceiling is approximately -15 kcal/mol (picomolar Kd).

USE AS A HARD GUARDRAIL:
  (a) |dG| should not exceed ~ 1.5 * min(HAC, 15) kcal/mol; any small-molecule prediction implying LE > 1.5 kcal/mol/atom is almost certainly a bug.
  (b) Any small-molecule prediction more negative than about -15 kcal/mol (Kd < ~1e-11 M) should be flagged. Documented natural exceptions exist -- Kuntz's own outliers include biotin-avidin (log K1 -13.43) and peptide phosphonates at carboxypeptidase (log K1 -13.96) -- so treat the ceiling as a trigger for human review, not a hard clamp.
  (c) Typical drug-like LE is ~0.3-0.5 kcal/mol/atom; fragments ~0.4-0.7. An emitted LE far outside 0.2-0.7 deserves scrutiny.
methods.coefficients: Initial slope ~= -1.5 kcal/mol per non-hydrogen atom; saturation at ~15 heavy atoms; ceiling ~= -15 kcal/mol. LE itself has no fitted coefficients -- it is a definition.
inputs_required: A predicted or measured dG (or Kd/Ki/IC50)
Heavy atom count of the ligand (trivial from RDKit: mol.GetNumHeavyAtoms())
methods.reported_accuracy: Not a predictor, so no RMSE applies. Kuntz et al. surveyed a large set of the strongest-binding known ligands (~68 distinct ligand-target pairs in their Table 1, spanning natural ligands, synthetic enzyme inhibitors, metal ions and small anions) to establish the empirical envelope.
methods.accuracy_dataset: Kuntz et al. 1999 Table 1 -- a curated survey of maximally potent ligands across many macromolecular targets.
methods.applicability_domain: Small molecules. Note the important criticism in the literature (Murcko, "Ligand efficiency metrics considered harmful", J Comput Aided Mol Des 2014) that LE is mathematically ill-behaved: because it divides a log-scale quantity by an atom count, LE depends on the arbitrary choice of standard-state concentration, and comparing LE between molecules of very different size is not rigorous. Use it as a smell test, not as an optimization objective. Does NOT apply to peptides or protein-protein interfaces, where per-atom efficiency is intrinsically much lower and a -15 kcal/mol ceiling is simply wrong (many PPIs are far tighter; TEM1/BLIP alone is ~-13.7 kcal/mol and avidin-biotin is ~-18 kcal/mol).
methods.implementation_route: Pure arithmetic. RDKit 2026.3.5 is already installed in the project venv at /Users/seunghojung/Documents/DeepMind_Bio/.venv/bin/python (verified: rdkit 2026.03.5, Python 3.14.6); heavy atom count via Chem.MolFromSmiles(smi).GetNumHeavyAtoms(). Microseconds.

energy.recommendation:
RECOMMENDED ARCHITECTURE FOR THE PLATFORM

Two separate pipelines, because the small-molecule and peptide/protein cases share no defensible method.

(b) PEPTIDE / PROTEIN bound to PROTEIN -- this is the case that is actually well served on a laptop.
Use PRODIGY (prodigy-prot 2.4.0). It is the only method in this survey that is (i) pip-installable with pure-Python deps, (ii) sub-second per complex, (iii) has a fully published closed-form equation I transcribed verbatim from the paper's MathML, and (iv) I verified end-to-end on this machine against two real complexes. Implement the equation directly rather than shelling out, but VALIDATE YOUR IMPLEMENTATION against the installed tool on a known complex before trusting it -- I did exactly this and it caught the sign inversion described in the warnings. Emit the PRODIGY simple models (contact-count, BSA) alongside as a consistency bracket; if they disagree with the full model by more than ~3 kcal/mol, flag the structure rather than emitting a number.

(a) SMALL MOLECULE bound to PROTEIN -- there is no good laptop-CPU answer, only defensible-with-caveats ones.
Ranked by defensibility per unit of engineering pain:
 1. RF-Score via `pip install oddt` -- best published accuracy of the laptop-feasible options (Rp 0.776, RMSE 1.58 log units on the PDBbind v2007 core set), pip-installable, milliseconds per complex, and RDKit is already in the project venv. Recommended default. (I verified it is on PyPI but did not install/run it -- do that before committing.)
 2. AutoDock Vina scoring function in --score_only rescoring mode. The coefficients I transcribed are complete and exact, so you can also just implement the ~60-line function yourself given XS atom typing, which sidesteps the install problem entirely. Its 2.85 kcal/mol standard error is honest and should be quoted with every value.
 3. PRODIGY-LIG (pip-installable, verified working, 0.24 s) as a cheap independent second opinion. RMSE 2.6 kcal/mol -- triage only.
 4. MM-GBSA via OpenMM only for a handful of high-value complexes, budgeting ~10 h of laptop CPU for a small system and days for a real target.
Do NOT put Boltz-2 or FEP on the laptop path.

INSTALL REALITY, MEASURED NOT ASSUMED: `pip install vina` FAILS on this machine (Apple M5 Max, Python 3.14) with "Boost library location was not found!". Confirmed via the PyPI JSON API that vina 1.2.7 publishes NO macOS wheels at all and nothing for Python >3.12. If the platform's install docs say "pip install vina", they are wrong on this hardware. Either pin the pipeline to conda-forge, ship your own implementation of the scoring function, or use ODDT/RF-Score which installs cleanly. Verified-installing-and-running on this machine: prodigy-prot 2.4.0, prodigy-lig 1.1.4, openmm 8.5.2, pdbfixer 1.12.0, biopython 1.88, freesasa 2.2.1.

CONFIDENCE HIERARCHY TO ENCODE IN THE UI. Every emitted number should carry its method's published RMSE and its dataset. Roughly: FEP ~1.1 kcal/mol (unavailable here) > PRODIGY 1.89 kcal/mol (protein-protein, in-domain) > RF-Score 1.58 log units ~ 2.16 kcal/mol (small molecule, PDBbind-family-biased) > PRODIGY contact/BSA simple models 2.08-2.46 kcal/mol > PRODIGY-LIG 2.6 kcal/mol > Vina 2.85 kcal/mol. Nothing available on this laptop is better than ~1.9 kcal/mol, which is a factor of ~25 in Kd. Design the UI so it is impossible to display more than one decimal place, and always show an interval, never a point estimate.

VALIDATION HARNESS I WOULD SHIP. Keep a small golden set with known experimental values and assert on every build, using the values I actually measured: 1YCR MDM2/p53 peptide -> PRODIGY -7.7 kcal/mol (exp ~-8.5 to -8.9); 1JTG TEM1/BLIP chains A vs B -> PRODIGY -11.6 kcal/mol (exp ~-13.7); 1STP streptavidin/biotin -> PRODIGY-LIG -7.15 kcal/mol (exp ~-18) -- keep this one specifically as the permanent reminder that these methods have catastrophic outliers.
