warnings: SIGN INVERSION IN THE PUBLISHED PRODIGY EQUATION -- THE SINGLE MOST DANGEROUS ITEM IN THIS REPORT. Equation 2 of Vangone & Bonvin 2015 as PRINTED returns a POSITIVE number and is not a binding free energy. The shipping reference implementation negates every one of the seven terms. If you transcribe the paper literally you will emit +7.7 kcal/mol where the correct answer is -7.7 kcal/mol, and if you then take exp(dG/RT) you will report a Kd of 4.5e5 M instead of 2.2e-6 M -- an error of eleven orders of magnitude that will look perfectly computed. I verified both branches numerically against the installed tool on 1YCR. Use the negated form.

DO NOT IMPLEMENT VINA'S ROTATABLE-BOND TERM AS AN ADDITION. Equation 9 of Trott & Olson is rendered as an IMAGE in the paper and is not machine-readable; when I asked a web-fetch summarizer to extract it, it returned 'g(c_inter) = c_inter + w*N_rot', which is WRONG. The reference implementation (conf_independent.cpp, num_tors_div) divides: s = c_inter / (1 + w_rot * N_rot). I derived this from the source substitution chain and it is unambiguous. This is exactly the reconstruction-from-a-summary failure mode the task warned about, and it happened on the very first fetch of this investigation.

A DOCKING SCORE IS NOT A FREE ENERGY. Vina reports its output in kcal/mol, which is a presentational choice, not a thermodynamic claim. The Vina scoring function contains NO electrostatics term and NO desolvation term -- stated outright in the Vina 1.2.0 paper ('Vina lacks electrostatics and solvation'). It has no explicit entropy term beyond a rotatable-bond divisor, no treatment of bridging waters, no protonation-state modeling, and no receptor flexibility. It is an empirical regression fitted to reproduce a ranking. Never write 'binding free energy' next to a Vina number; write 'Vina score (arbitrary units, kcal/mol-like)'.

THE EMPIRICAL CORRELATION BETWEEN DOCKING SCORE AND MEASURED AFFINITY IS WEAK, AND THIS IS THE HEADLINE CAVEAT. Vina's own reported standard error is 2.85 kcal/mol -- a factor of ~120 in Kd, i.e. the method cannot reliably distinguish a 1 nM binder from a 100 nM binder. Across the docking literature the score-vs-affinity Pearson r for a general scoring function on a diverse set is typically 0.4-0.6, and drops sharply on any single target where the dynamic range is narrow -- exactly the lead-optimization situation people want to use it for. Docking is a POSE-PREDICTION and ENRICHMENT tool that happens to emit a number; it is not an affinity predictor. Vina's own DUD-E results make this concrete: mean AUC 0.71 but standard deviation 0.15, and for 17 of 50 targets BEDROC < 0.1, i.e. no useful enrichment at all.

NEVER RANK ACROSS TARGETS WITH ANY OF THESE METHODS. Every scoring function here has systematic per-target bias, and every one correlates strongly with ligand size / interface size. Comparing a Vina score for target X against a Vina score for target Y is meaningless. Comparing PRODIGY values between a 200-residue and a 900-residue complex is likewise dominated by the size term, not by interaction quality. Ranking within a single target with a fixed protocol is the only defensible use.

PRODIGY IS OUT OF ITS TRAINING DOMAIN FOR PEPTIDES. Its 81-complex training set consists of globular protein-protein complexes from the Kastritis benchmark and contains no short peptides. Two structural reasons it should degrade: the %NIS terms are near-meaningless for a peptide whose entire surface is interface, and the model has no term for the large conformational-entropy penalty a disordered peptide pays on binding, which is often the dominant contribution. My own two measurements were both underbound by 1-2 kcal/mol. Report peptide predictions with an error bar of at least +/-1.9 kcal/mol and label them off-domain.

CONTACT-BASED AND BURIED-SURFACE-AREA ESTIMATORS ARE ORDER-OF-MAGNITUDE TOOLS ONLY. From the PRODIGY paper's own Table 3: a pure BSA model achieves R = -0.46 (R^2 = 0.21, i.e. it explains 21% of the variance) with RMSE 2.46 kcal/mol; a pure contact count achieves R = -0.59 (R^2 = 0.35) with RMSE 2.25 kcal/mol. An RMSE of 2.5 kcal/mol is a factor of ~65 in Kd. These correlate with affinity largely because both correlate with complex size, so they carry almost no information about interface QUALITY and cannot distinguish a good interface from a large bad one. Never use them to rank close analogues.

THESE ARE ALL RESCORING METHODS AND THEY INHERIT 100% OF THE POSE ERROR. PRODIGY, PRODIGY-LIG, RF-Score, NNScore and MM-GBSA all take a 3D complex as input and have no mechanism to detect that the pose is wrong. If the platform feeds them AlphaFold3 or docked models rather than crystal structures, the reported accuracy figures DO NOT APPLY -- PRODIGY-LIG's own numbers show the size of this effect: Kendall tau 0.37 on docked models versus 0.43 on crystal structures for the same 102 D3R complexes. Always propagate and display the pose confidence (pLDDT/ipTM/PAE) alongside the affinity, and refuse to emit an affinity below a pose-confidence threshold.

SILENT WRONG-INTERFACE FAILURE. I hit this live: 1JTG contains two copies of the TEM1/BLIP complex in the asymmetric unit, and selecting chains A,B versus C,D scores a CRYSTAL CONTACT, returning -7.0 kcal/mol instead of the correct -11.6 kcal/mol. No warning, no error, a plausible-looking number. Any automated pipeline must resolve the biological assembly (PDB assembly 1 / PISA) rather than naively taking the first two chains.

CATASTROPHIC OUTLIERS EXIST AND THE METHODS CANNOT FLAG THEM. I measured PRODIGY-LIG at -7.15 kcal/mol for streptavidin-biotin (1STP) against an experimental ~-18 kcal/mol -- an ~11 kcal/mol, seven-orders-of-magnitude error. An RMSE is an average; the tail is much worse than the RMSE suggests. Any single prediction can be this wrong, and nothing in the method's output signals it.

UNIT AND SCALE CONFUSION IS A REAL SOURCE OF SILENT ERROR. RF-Score's 1.58 is in log Kd units, NOT kcal/mol (multiply by 1.364 at 298 K to get ~2.16 kcal/mol). Boltz-2 emits log10 of concentration in MICROMOLAR, not molar, and is trained on pooled Ki/Kd/IC50/EC50/AC50, so its target variable is not a single physical quantity -- an IC50 is assay- and substrate-concentration-dependent and is not a binding constant. PRODIGY's %NIS terms are PERCENTAGES on a 0-100 scale, not fractions; passing 0.315 instead of 31.51 will silently produce a wrong answer of plausible magnitude. Vina's N_rot counts ACTIVE rotatable bonds between heavy atoms, not all rotatable bonds. PRODIGY's Kd conversion uses R = 0.0019858775 kcal/mol/K and T in Kelvin from a Celsius input.

COEFFICIENTS I COULD NOT FULLY VERIFY, FLAGGED SO THEY ARE NOT USED BY ACCIDENT. (1) Vinardo: I retrieved only weight_gauss1 = -0.045 and weight_rot = 0.05846 from source; the repulsion, hydrophobic and hydrogen weights are UNVERIFIED -- re-read src/lib/vina.h before using Vinardo. (2) NNScore 2.0: the widely circulated Pearson 0.629 / RMSE 1.391 figures could NOT be traced to the primary paper and the dataset is unidentified -- do not quote them. (3) Smina's CSAR-2010-refitted custom weight vector was not retrieved (paywalled at ACS). (4) Quiroga & Villarreal's Vinardo accuracy figures were not retrieved. (5) Gaillard 2018's exact CASF-2013 scoring-power Pearson r for Vina was not retrieved -- only the qualitative statement that Vina ranks in the first quarter of CASF-2013 methods and is best in docking power. In all five cases: NOT RETRIEVED, do not reconstruct.

TWO INTERNAL INCONSISTENCIES IN THE PRODIGY PAPERS THAT WILL CONFUSE ANY IMPLEMENTER. (1) eLife 2015 Table 3 Model 6 lists slope magnitudes (0.09420, 0.10038, 0.19522, 0.22609, 0.18786, 0.13872) that differ in the 3rd-4th decimal from Equation 2 (0.09459, 0.10007, 0.19577, 0.22671, 0.18681, 0.13810), although both share intercept 15.9433. Equation 2 is what the software implements and what I verified reproduces the tool output exactly; use Equation 2. (2) In the PRODIGY-LIG paper, Eq. 3's -0.1277895 term is printed against AC_CC but the reference code applies it to AC_XX; the code is almost certainly right given Eqs. 1 and 2 both attach large negative coefficients to AC_XX. Trust the code over the PDF in both cases, and verify.

PDBbind CORE-SET ACCURACY FIGURES ARE OPTIMISTIC. RF-Score's headline Rp = 0.776 is on the PDBbind v2007 core set, which shares protein families with its training set (the refined set minus core). Independent evaluations on target-disjoint splits consistently show substantially worse generalization for ML scoring functions. Treat 0.776 as an upper bound achievable only for protein families well represented in PDBbind, and expect materially worse performance on a novel target -- which is precisely the situation a discovery platform is in.

MM-GBSA IS NOT AS PRECISE AS ITS DECIMAL PLACES SUGGEST. Genheden & Ryde report that independent MM/PBSA calculations of the SAME system can differ by more than 10 kcal/mol for small-molecule complexes -- the run-to-run precision can be worse than the entire dynamic range of interest. The result depends strongly on the interior dielectric constant, the GB model, MD length (longer is not always better) and snapshot count, none of which have a principled default. The entropy term is almost always omitted in practice, in which case the computed quantity is an enthalpy-like interaction energy and MUST NOT be labelled a free energy. Their expert opinion further notes that most attempts to improve the method with QM, polarizable force fields or better solvation have DETERIORATED the results.

DO NOT CLAIM FEP-LIKE ACCURACY FROM ANY LAPTOP METHOD. FEP itself, the most rigorous practical method, achieves RMSE 1.1 kcal/mol (Wang 2015; Abel 2017 average 1.1, median 1.0, average R^2 0.57) -- roughly a 6x error in Kd. Nothing on a laptop CPU beats this. Any pipeline output claiming sub-kcal/mol accuracy is either mis-scaled or overfit. Concretely, one relative FEP transformation needs ~120-240 ns of explicit-solvent sampling; extrapolating from my measured 11.4 ns/day on a 1,670-atom implicit-solvent system, that is on the order of 300-600 days of CPU on this machine versus a few hours on a GPU.

BOLTZ-2 AND GNINA DO NOT MEET THE LAPTOP-CPU REQUIREMENT AS STATED. Boltz-2 needs a CUDA GPU for usable throughput and this machine exposes only Reference/CPU/OpenCL platforms. gnina is officially Linux-only (Docker on macOS), is not pip-installable, and its 1.3 paper reports NO Pearson r or RMSE for its CNNaffinity head -- so there is currently no citable affinity accuracy for gnina. Note also that gnina's CNNscore is a pose-quality probability in [0,1], NOT an affinity; confusing CNNscore with CNNaffinity is an easy and serious mistake.

LIGAND EFFICIENCY IS A SMELL TEST, NOT AN OBJECTIVE. LE is mathematically ill-behaved (Murcko, 'Ligand efficiency metrics considered harmful', 2014): it divides a log-scale quantity by an atom count, so it depends on the arbitrary standard-state concentration and is not rigorous to compare across molecules of very different size. Use the Kuntz ceiling (~-1.5 kcal/mol per heavy atom, saturating at ~15 atoms and ~-15 kcal/mol) to FLAG implausible small-molecule outputs for human review, not to clamp them -- Kuntz's own dataset contains legitimate outliers. And do not apply the -15 kcal/mol ceiling to peptides or protein-protein interfaces at all: many PPIs are far tighter (TEM1/BLIP ~-13.7, avidin-biotin ~-18 kcal/mol).

PIP-INSTALLABILITY IS NOT A STABLE PROPERTY -- VERIFY ON THE TARGET MACHINE, NOT FROM DOCUMENTATION. The vina failure here was caused purely by the combination of Apple Silicon and Python 3.14, neither of which the package publishes wheels for. Any 'runnable_locally: true' claim in this report that I did not personally execute (RF-Score/ODDT, smina, gnina, Vinardo) should be re-verified in the platform's actual deployment environment before being written into user-facing docs.

methods.name: CNS MPO (Wager desirability)
methods.paper: Wager TT, Hou X, Verhoest PR, Villalobos A. "Moving beyond Rules: The Development of a Central Nervous System Multiparameter Optimization (CNS MPO) Approach To Enable Alignment of Druglike Properties." ACS Chem Neurosci 2010;1(6):435-449. Transforms reprinted as Figure 1 of Wager TT et al. "Central Nervous System Multiparameter Optimization Desirability: Application in Drug Discovery." ACS Chem Neurosci 2016;7(6):767-775 (ACS Editors' Choice, open access) — this is the copy I actually fetched and read.
methods.equation:
CNS MPO = T0(ClogP) + T0(ClogD) + T0(MW) + T0(TPSA) + T0(HBD) + T0(pKa), each T0 in [0,1], equally weighted, total range 0-6.

Two transform shapes, both piecewise LINEAR between inflection points (paper text 2016: "A monotonic decreasing function was used for ClogP, ClogD, MW, pKa, and HBD, whereas a hump function was used to define TPSA... Each parameter was weighted equally, and the collective score ranged from 0 to 6").

MONOTONIC DECREASING, params (g = green/most-desirable point where T0=1.0, r = red/least-desirable point where T0=0.0):
  T0(x) = 1                     if x <= g
  T0(x) = 1 - (x - g)/(r - g)   if g < x < r
  T0(x) = 0                     if x >= r

HUMP (TPSA only), params (r1=20, g1=40, g2=90, r2=120):
  T0(x) = 0                        if x <= 20 or x >= 120
  T0(x) = (x - 20)/(40 - 20)       if 20 < x < 40
  T0(x) = 1                        if 40 <= x <= 90
  T0(x) = 1 - (x - 90)/(120 - 90)  if 90 < x < 120

NOTE ON HBD — this is the one place a naive reading gets it wrong. Figure 1E marks the green arrow at HBD=0 and the red arrow at HBD=4, but the plotted per-molecule T0 values are 1.00, 0.83, 0.50, 0.17, 0.00, 0.00 for HBD = 0,1,2,3,4,5. A straight line from (0,1) to (4,0) would give 1.00, 0.75, 0.50, 0.25, 0.00 and does NOT reproduce the paper. The parameterization g=0.5, r=3.5 reproduces the published points exactly: 1-(1-0.5)/3 = 0.8333, 1-(2-0.5)/3 = 0.5000, 1-(3-0.5)/3 = 0.1667, clipped to [0,1] at the ends. Verified numerically.
methods.coefficients:
Read directly off Figure 1 of Wager 2016 (image downloaded at 1000x994 and read; panels A-F):
  (A) ClogP: green 3, red 5    -> T0=1 at ClogP<=3, 0 at >=5 (ClogP 4 -> 0.5)
  (B) ClogD(pH 7.4): green 2, red 4
  (C) MW: green 360, red 500
  (D) TPSA: red 20, green 40, green 90, red 120 (hump; TPSA 30 -> 0.5, TPSA 105 -> 0.5)
  (E) HBD: green 0, red 4 as arrow labels; implement as g=0.5, r=3.5 to reproduce the plotted points (see equation note)
  (F) most basic pKa: green 8, red 10 (pKa 9 -> 0.5)
Decision cut-off in common use: CNS MPO >= 4.0 (Wager 2010: "74% of marketed CNS drugs... displayed a high CNS MPO score (MPO desirability score >= 4, using a scale of 0-6)").
inputs_required: pKa of the most basic centre
methods.reported_accuracy: The 2010/2016 papers report enrichment, not a classification metric: 74% of marketed CNS drugs scored >=4 on a 0-6 scale. An INDEPENDENT external evaluation reports CNS MPO AUC = 0.61 for separating CNS from non-CNS drugs, versus AUC = 0.86 for the Gupta BBB Score and 0.67 for MPO_V2 (Gupta M et al. J Med Chem 2019;62:9824-9836, reproduced in Mittal et al. Molecules 2024;29:1264, which I fetched). This is a weak classifier.
methods.accuracy_dataset: Wager: 119 marketed CNS drugs + 108 Pfizer CNS clinical candidates (plus 21 post-implementation candidates in the 2016 follow-up). Gupta/Mittal AUC comparison: curated set of 320 CNS and 770 non-CNS drugs, restricted to passive-diffusion CNS drugs with documented active-transport cases removed.
methods.applicability_domain: Small-molecule CNS drugs and clinical candidates, median MW 305.3 Da, median TPSA 44.8 A^2, median HBD 1, median ClogP 2.8, median ClogD 1.7, median pKa 8.4. It is a medicinal-chemistry heuristic, explicitly NOT a QSAR/ML model (2016 paper: "In contrast to a quantitative structure-activity relationship or machine learning model, the CNS MPO desirability tool is built upon medicinal chemistry experience"). Score is highly sensitive to which ClogD and pKa calculator you use — the 2016 authors say so themselves. No lower bounds on any property, so trivially small fragments score 6.
methods.implementation_route: Implement the formula directly (~30 lines). ClogP/MW/TPSA/HBD from RDKit (Crippen.MolLogP, Descriptors.MolWt, MolSurf.TPSA, rdMolDescriptors.CalcNumHBD). ClogD(7.4) and most-basic pKa are NOT in RDKit — you must supply them from an external predictor (ChemAxon cxcalc, MoKa, ACD, or an open pKa model) and you must record which one, because the score moves with it. methods.name: Lipinski Rule of 5
methods.paper: Lipinski CA, Lombardo F, Dominy BW, Feeney PJ. "Experimental and computational approaches to estimate solubility and permeability in drug discovery and development settings." Adv Drug Deliv Rev 2001;46(1-3):3-26 (reprint of Adv Drug Deliv Rev 1997;23:3-25).
methods.equation:
Verbatim from the abstract I fetched: "the rule of 5 predicts that poor absorption or permeation is more likely when there are more than 5 H-bond donors, 10 H-bond acceptors, the molecular weight (MWT) is greater than 500 and the calculated Log P (CLogP) is greater than 5 (or MlogP > 4.15)".

Implement as violation count (0-4): HBD > 5; HBA > 10; MW > 500; ClogP > 5 (or MLogP > 4.15). Conventional pass = <= 1 violation.
methods.coefficients: HBD 5; HBA 10; MW 500 Da; CLogP 5; MLogP 4.15 (alternative lipophilicity criterion, from the same sentence).
methods.reported_accuracy: None. The 1997/2001 paper reports no AUC/sensitivity/specificity — it is a distributional observation about the 90th-percentile boundaries of the USAN/INN orally-administered drug set. Any AUC quoted for 'Ro5' comes from a later re-evaluation, not from Lipinski.
methods.accuracy_dataset: World Drug Index subset of compounds that had entered Phase II (USAN/INN names), ~2,245 compounds.
methods.applicability_domain: Orally administered small molecules crossing membranes by PASSIVE diffusion. Lipinski explicitly excluded substrates of biological transporters, and excluded antibiotics, antifungals, vitamins and cardiac glycosides as known exception classes. It says nothing about parenteral drugs, and nothing about peptides.
methods.implementation_route: Direct implementation over RDKit descriptors. Note RDKit's Lipinski.NumHAcceptors uses a different HBA definition than Lipinski's raw N+O count — pick one and document it.

methods.name: Veber rules
methods.paper: Veber DF, Johnson SR, Cheng HY, Smith BR, Ward KW, Kopple KD. "Molecular properties that influence the oral bioavailability of drug candidates." J Med Chem 2002;45(12):2615-2623.
methods.equation:
Verbatim from the abstract I fetched: "compounds which meet only the two criteria of (1) 10 or fewer rotatable bonds and (2) polar surface area equal to or less than 140 A(2) (or 12 or fewer H-bond donors and acceptors) will have a high probability of good oral bioavailability in the rat".

Pass if: nRotB <= 10 AND (TPSA <= 140 OR (HBD + HBA) <= 12).
methods.coefficients: Rotatable bonds 10; PSA 140 A^2; total H-bond count (donors + acceptors) 12.
methods.reported_accuracy: No AUC reported. The claim is a probability statement over the internal dataset; the paper also states that "The commonly applied molecular weight cutoff at 500 does not itself significantly separate compounds with poor oral bioavailability from those with acceptable values in this extensive data set."
methods.accuracy_dataset: Oral bioavailability measurements in RATS for over 1,100 SmithKline Beecham/GSK drug candidates.
methods.applicability_domain: Rat oral bioavailability of small-molecule drug candidates. Species-specific; rat-to-human extrapolation is an added assumption the paper does not make.
methods.implementation_route: RDKit: rdMolDescriptors.CalcNumRotatableBonds, MolSurf.TPSA, CalcNumHBD/CalcNumHBA. Trivial.

methods.name: Egan egg
methods.paper: Egan WJ, Merz KM Jr, Baldwin JJ. "Prediction of drug absorption using multivariate statistics." J Med Chem 2000;43(21):3867-3877.
methods.equation:
EQUATION NOT RETRIEVED. The paper is not open access (checked Unpaywall: is_oa = false, no OA locations) and I could not obtain the full text. What the abstract confirms: "The descriptors chosen for inclusion in the model were PSA and AlogP98", built by "robust outlier detection" pattern recognition — i.e. the model is a robust-covariance confidence ellipse in (PSA, AlogP98) space, NOT a rectangular cutoff pair. I did not retrieve the ellipse centre, covariance matrix, or confidence level.

What is widely IMPLEMENTED under the name 'Egan' (e.g. in SwissADME) is a rectangular approximation: WLOGP <= 5.88 AND TPSA <= 131.6. I could not trace those two numbers to a passage in Egan's paper. Treat them as SwissADME's operationalisation, not as Egan's published model. Do not present them as 'the Egan ellipse'.

Relevant corroborating primary statement, from the BOILED-Egg Supporting Information which I did fetch and read: "In contrast to the Egan egg, all our tentative ellipses were evaluated according to their ability to include as many HIA+ ... and to exclude as many HIA- ... as possible", and "the computation of the ellipse took into account well-absorbed molecules but neglected poorly absorbed molecules. The resulting confidence region merely depicts the dispersion of properties related to good absorption and lacks an assessment of accuracy." Daina & Zoete are stating that the Egan egg has no published accuracy assessment.
methods.coefficients: NOT RETRIEVED from primary source. SwissADME operational cutoffs (secondary, unverified against Egan): WLOGP <= 5.88, TPSA <= 131.6.
methods.reported_accuracy: Abstract states "a good rate of successful predictions (74-92%, depending on the dataset and exact criterion used)". No AUC, no sensitivity/specificity breakdown retrieved.
methods.accuracy_dataset: Literature compounds well- and poorly-absorbed in humans, plus validation on "hundreds of known orally delivered drugs, 'drug-like' molecules, and Pharmacopeia, Inc. compounds, which had been assayed for Caco-2 cell permeability". Exact n not retrieved.
methods.applicability_domain: Passive intestinal absorption of small molecules. Actively transported compounds were identified as OUTLIERS and removed during model construction, so actively transported and effluxed compounds are out of domain by construction.
methods.implementation_route: If you want an egg, use the BOILED-Egg instead: its ellipse parameters ARE published and I retrieved them. Only implement 'Egan' if you label it explicitly as the SwissADME two-cutoff approximation.

methods.name: Ghose filter
methods.paper: Ghose AK, Viswanadhan VN, Wendoloski JJ. "A knowledge-based approach in designing combinatorial or medicinal chemistry libraries for drug discovery. 1. A qualitative and quantitative characterization of known drug databases." J Comb Chem 1999;1(1):55-68.
methods.equation:
Verbatim from the abstract I fetched: "For the CMC database, the qualifying range (covering more than 80% of the compounds) of the calculated log P is between -0.4 and 5.6, with an average value of 2.52. For molecular weight, the qualifying range is between 160 and 480, with an average value of 357. For molar refractivity, the qualifying range is between 40 and 130, with an average value of 97. For the total number of atoms, the qualifying range is between 20 and 70, with an average value of 48."

Pass if: -0.4 <= AlogP <= 5.6 AND 160 <= MW <= 480 AND 40 <= MR <= 130 AND 20 <= nAtoms <= 70.
methods.coefficients: AlogP [-0.4, 5.6] (mean 2.52); MW [160, 480] (mean 357); molar refractivity [40, 130] (mean 97); total atom count [20, 70] (mean 48). All are the >80%-coverage qualifying ranges of the CMC database.
methods.reported_accuracy: None reported. These are descriptive percentile ranges of a drug database, not a validated classifier. The 'accuracy' is definitional: the ranges cover >80% of CMC compounds.
methods.accuracy_dataset: Comprehensive Medicinal Chemistry (CMC) database and seven therapeutic-class subsets (including a CNS-active subset).
methods.applicability_domain: Small drug-like molecules of the late-1990s CMC database. A library-design filter, not a pharmacokinetic model.
methods.implementation_route: RDKit: Crippen.MolLogP (Wildman-Crippen, close to but not identical to Ghose-Crippen AlogP), Crippen.MolMR, Descriptors.MolWt, and mol.GetNumAtoms() on the H-ADDED molecule (Chem.AddHs) — the paper's atom count includes hydrogens.

methods.name: Muegge pharmacophore-point filter
methods.paper: Muegge I, Heald SL, Brittelli D. "Simple selection criteria for drug-like chemical matter." J Med Chem 2001;44(12):1841-1846.
methods.equation:
EQUATION NOT RETRIEVED. The paper is not open access (Unpaywall: is_oa = false) and the abstract does not contain the numeric criteria — it only says "A simple pharmacophore point filter has been developed... a minimum count of well-defined pharmacophore points is required to pass the filter." I did not obtain the criteria table.

The criteria commonly implemented under the name 'Muegge' (SwissADME and clones) are: 200 <= MW <= 600; -2 <= XLOGP3 <= 5; TPSA <= 150; number of rings <= 7; number of carbon atoms > 4; number of heteroatoms > 1; rotatable bonds <= 15; HBA <= 10; HBD <= 5. I could NOT verify these against the primary paper. Do not present them as transcribed from Muegge et al.
methods.coefficients: NOT RETRIEVED from primary source. Secondary (SwissADME operationalisation) values listed above, unverified.
methods.reported_accuracy: From the abstract: "The application of the filter results in 66-69% of subsets of the MDDR database to be classified as drug-like. Furthermore, 61-68% of subsets of the CMC database are classified as drug-like. In contrast, only 36% of the ACD are found to be drug-like." These are pass rates, not classification metrics.
methods.accuracy_dataset: MDDR, CMC and ACD (Available Chemicals Directory) databases.
methods.applicability_domain: Discriminating drug-like from non-drug-like chemical matter in screening libraries. It says nothing about ADME endpoints and predicts no PK parameter.
methods.implementation_route: If you implement it, label it 'Muegge (SwissADME operationalisation)' and flag the provenance gap in code comments. XLOGP3 is not in RDKit; substituting Crippen MolLogP changes the result.

methods.name: Pfizer 3/75 rule
methods.paper: Hughes JD, Blagg J, Price DA, Bailey S, et al. "Physiochemical drug properties associated with in vivo toxicological outcomes." Bioorg Med Chem Lett 2008;18(17):4872-4875. Definition quoted from the peer-reviewed source I actually read: Yukawa T et al. "Utility of Physicochemical Properties for the Prediction of Toxicological Outcomes: Takeda Perspective." ACS Med Chem Lett 2020;11(2):203-209 (PMC7025387, open access).
methods.paper_id: 10.1016/j.bmcl.2008.07.071, PMID 18691886 (primary); 10.1021/acsmedchemlett.9b00536, PMC7025387 (source of the quoted definition)
methods.equation:
Verbatim from Yukawa et al. describing Hughes et al.: "Pfizer scientists carried out an analysis of 245 compounds with exploratory toxicology study data and suggested that drug candidates in the chemical space of low ClogP (less than 3) and high TPSA (more than 75) are considerably less likely to cause significant toxicological effects at total plasma concentrations below 10 uM (referred to as the 3/75 rule). They showed that compounds with this low-ClogP/high-TPSA profile are approximately 2.5 times more likely to be clean as to be toxic."

Implement as a 2x2 quadrant flag, not a score:
  LOW RISK  quadrant: ClogP < 3 AND TPSA > 75
  HIGH RISK quadrant: ClogP > 3 AND TPSA < 75
  (the two off-diagonal quadrants are intermediate/unassigned)
methods.coefficients: ClogP threshold 3; TPSA threshold 75 A^2; reported odds ~2.5-fold (clean:toxic) in the favourable quadrant; exposure context total plasma Cmax 10 uM.
methods.reported_accuracy: ~2.5x odds ratio (clean vs toxic) for the low-ClogP/high-TPSA quadrant. Not an AUC. The Takeda replication on 284 internal compounds reproduced the lipophilicity trend but showed it is ionisation-state dependent, and notes "the Pfizer data set was biased toward lipophilic basic molecules. Indeed, 73% of compounds within the data set that had values of ClogP > 3 and PSA < 75 were categorized as 'basic molecule'."
methods.accuracy_dataset: 245 preclinical Pfizer compounds with in vivo toleration (IVT) study data in animals. Replication: 284 Takeda internal compounds, rat/mouse in vivo tox with matched Cmax.
methods.applicability_domain: Preclinical small-molecule candidates with in vivo animal toleration data, biased toward lipophilic bases. It is an odds statement about a population, not a per-compound prediction. Applying it to one molecule as a yes/no toxicity call misuses the source.
methods.implementation_route: Two RDKit descriptors and a quadrant assignment. Report the quadrant plus the odds ratio, never a probability of toxicity for the specific compound.

methods.name: GSK 4/400 rule
methods.paper: Gleeson MP. "Generation of a set of simple, interpretable ADMET rules of thumb." J Med Chem 2008;51(4):817-834.
methods.equation:
EQUATION NOT RETRIEVED. Not open access (Unpaywall: is_oa = false) and the abstract does not state the numbers. The abstract does state the qualitative conclusion verbatim: "almost all ADMET parameters deteriorate with either increasing molecular weight, logP, or both, with ionization state playing either a beneficial or detrimental affect depending on the parameter in question. This study re-emphasizes the need to focus on a lower molecular weight and logP area of physicochemical property space to obtain improved ADMET parameters."

The rule as universally implemented is: MW <= 400 AND logP <= 4. I did not read that sentence in Gleeson's paper, so I am not certifying the 400/4 pair as a transcription. If you implement it, cite it as 'the GSK 4/400 rule of thumb, commonly attributed to Gleeson 2008' and note the primary text was not retrieved.
methods.coefficients: NOT VERIFIED against primary. Conventional values: MW 400 Da, logP 4.
inputs_required: ionisation state (acid/base/neutral/zwitterion) for the full Gleeson analysis
methods.reported_accuracy: None retrievable. The paper reports trends across ten GSK ADMET assays (solubility, permeability, bioavailability, Vd, PPB, CNS penetration, brain tissue binding, P-gp efflux, hERG inhibition, and CYP1A2/2C9/2C19/2D6/3A4 inhibition), not a classifier metric.
methods.accuracy_dataset: Internal GSK ADMET assay datasets across the ten assays listed above. Sizes not retrieved.
methods.applicability_domain: Small-molecule lead optimisation. Explicitly ionisation-state dependent — a single MW/logP cutoff pair discards the paper's main message.
methods.implementation_route: Trivial to implement; the issue is provenance, not code. Either obtain the paper and transcribe the actual values, or label 400/4 as folklore.

methods.name: QED (Quantitative Estimate of Drug-likeness)
methods.paper: Bickerton GR, Paolini GV, Besnard J, Muresan S, Hopkins AL. "Quantifying the chemical beauty of drugs." Nat Chem 2012;4(2):90-98. Coefficients transcribed from the reference implementation in RDKit (rdkit/Chem/QED.py, Novartis/Biscu-it), cross-checked against the paper's weight table via PMC3524573.
methods.equation:
Eight ADS (asymmetric double sigmoidal) desirability functions, combined as a WEIGHTED GEOMETRIC MEAN.

ADS, exactly as coded in RDKit QED.py:
  exp1 = 1 + exp(-(x - C + D/2)/E)
  exp2 = 1 + exp(-(x - C - D/2)/F)
  dx   = A + (B/exp1) * (1 - 1/exp2)
  d(x) = dx / DMAX          # DMAX normalises the ADS peak to 1

QED:
  QED_w = exp( sum_i w_i * ln(d_i) / sum_i w_i )
(the paper writes it as "QED_w = exp[Sum(w_i*ln d_i) / Sum w_i]", confirmed against PMC3524573).
inputs_required: HBA (QED's own 11-SMARTS acceptor definition, NOT RDKit's default HBA)
Aromatic ring count (SSSR after deleting aliphatic rings)
methods.reported_accuracy: QED is a desirability index, not a predictor — no RMSE/AUC applies. RDKit warns its values "are not completely identical to those from the original publication" because of logP calculator differences. I verified the three anchor molecules in the RDKit docstring reproduce the published reference values: 0.2531 (ref 0.253), 0.2347 (ref 0.234), 0.2349 (ref 0.234).
methods.accuracy_dataset: ADS functions fitted to the property distributions of 771 orally administered small-molecule drugs from DrugBank; weights derived from a study in which 79 medicinal chemists rated 17,000 molecules for attractiveness.
methods.applicability_domain: Oral small-molecule drugs. Every one of the eight ADS curves was fitted to that distribution, so QED is a similarity-to-oral-small-molecule-drugs score by construction. Outside that chemotype it returns a near-zero value that is an artefact of the curve tails, not an assessment.
methods.implementation_route: Already installed: from rdkit.Chem import QED; QED.qed(mol) (default weights_mean), plus QED.weights_max, QED.weights_none, QED.properties. Module path on this machine: /Users/seunghojung/Documents/DeepMind_Bio/.venv/lib/python3.14/site-packages/rdkit/Chem/QED.py

methods.name: SAscore (synthetic accessibility)
methods.paper: Ertl P, Schuffenhauer A. "Estimation of synthetic accessibility score of drug-like molecules based on molecular complexity and fragment contributions." J Cheminform 2009;1:8. Code transcribed from the RDKit Contrib implementation by Ertl & Landrum.
methods.equation:
sascore_raw = score1 + score2 + score3, then rescaled to 1-10.

score1 (fragment score) = sum over Morgan-radius-2 sparse COUNT fingerprint bits of (fragment_score[bit] * count) / total_count; unseen bits get -4.

score2 (complexity penalty) = -(sizePenalty + stereoPenalty + spiroPenalty + bridgePenalty + macrocyclePenalty) where
  sizePenalty       = nAtoms**1.005 - nAtoms
  stereoPenalty     = log10(nChiralCenters + 1)
  spiroPenalty      = log10(nSpiro + 1)
  bridgePenalty     = log10(nBridgeheads + 1)
  macrocyclePenalty = log10(2) if any ring size > 8 else 0     # DEVIATES from the paper, which defines log10(nMacrocycles+1)

score3 (symmetry / fingerprint-density correction, NOT in the paper, added in v1.1) = 0.5*log(nAtoms/numBits) if nAtoms > numBits else 0

Rescale:
  sascore = 11 - (raw - (-4.0) + 1)/(2.5 - (-4.0)) * 9
  if sascore > 8: sascore = 8 + log(sascore + 1 - 9)
  clip to [1, 10]
methods.coefficients: min = -4.0, max = 2.5, span 9, offset 11 in the rescaling; unknown-fragment penalty -4; size exponent 1.005; macrocycle penalty log10(2); symmetry factor 0.5; Morgan radius 2. Fragment contribution table = fpscores.pkl.gz shipped with RDKit, derived from 1 million PubChem compounds in the original work.
methods.reported_accuracy: Original paper: correlation of SAscore with medicinal chemists' manual synthesis-difficulty ratings, r^2 = 0.89 on a set of 40 molecules. The RDKit header states: "for a set of 10k diverse molecules the agreement between the original method as implemented in PipelinePilot and this implementation is r2 = 0.97" — note this second figure is code-to-code agreement, not accuracy.
methods.accuracy_dataset: Fragment contributions from 1 million PubChem compounds; chemist-rating validation set of 40 molecules; 10k diverse molecules for the implementation-agreement check.
methods.applicability_domain: Drug-like organic small molecules. For a synthetic peptide the score is meaningless in the intended sense — SAscore measures difficulty of bespoke organic synthesis, whereas peptides are made by SPPS at roughly constant per-residue effort. Long peptides incur large size penalties and saturate near 10 for reasons unrelated to real synthetic difficulty.
methods.implementation_route: RDKit Contrib, present on this machine at /Users/seunghojung/Documents/DeepMind_Bio/.venv/lib/python3.14/site-packages/rdkit/Contrib/SA_Score/sascorer.py (plus fpscores.pkl.gz). Import via sys.path.append(os.path.join(RDConfig.RDContribDir,'SA_Score')); import sascorer; sascorer.calculateScore(mol). Verified: aspirin 1.580, nicotine 2.500.

methods.name: BOILED-Egg (Brain Or IntestinaL EstimateD permeation)
methods.paper: Daina A, Zoete V. "A BOILED-Egg To Predict Gastrointestinal Absorption and Brain Penetration of Small Molecules." ChemMedChem 2016;11(11):1117-1121. Ellipse parameters transcribed from the Supporting Information (Data S1, Data S2, Figure S1 and Figure S2 captions), downloaded via the Europe PMC supplementary-files endpoint for PMC5089604 (file CMDC-11-1117-s001.pdf) and extracted.
methods.equation:
Two rotated ellipses in the (tPSA on x, WLOGP on y) plane. A molecule is inside an ellipse iff, with a = major/2, b = minor/2, theta = angle in radians:
  u =  (tPSA - cx)*cos(theta) + (WLOGP - cy)*sin(theta)
  v = -(tPSA - cx)*sin(theta) + (WLOGP - cy)*cos(theta)
  inside  <=>  u^2/a^2 + v^2/b^2 <= 1

Interpretation (paper): "The white region is the physicochemical space of molecules with highest probability of being absorbed by the gastrointestinal tract, and the yellow region (yolk) is the physicochemical space of molecules with highest probability to permeate to the brain. Yolk and white areas are not mutually exclusive."

The ellipses were NOT derived as statistical confidence regions. They are Monte-Carlo optimised classifiers: "Five parameters defining the ellipse - the Cartesian coordinates of the foci (x1, x2); (y1, y2) and the major axis (or largest diameter, d) - were submitted to Monte-Carlo (MC) optimization, evaluated by the Matthews correlation coefficient... After about 100 000 independent MC runs of 100 000 cycles each".
methods.coefficients:
DENORMALISED ellipses, verbatim from SI Figure S1/S2 captions:

  HIA / white ellipse:  centre at (71.051; 2.292); length of major axis = 142.081; length of minor axis = 8.740; angle: -1.031325 degrees.
  BBB / yolk ellipse:   centre at (38.117; 3.177); length of major axis = 82.061;  length of minor axis = 5.557; angle: -0.171887 degrees.

Self-consistency check I ran: those parameters reproduce the SI's stated bounding boxes to 2 dp. HIA computed extents tPSA 0.02-142.08, WLOGP -2.26 to 6.84 vs paper's "tPSA ranges between 0.0 and 142.1 A2 and WLOGP between -2.3 and 6.8". BBB computed extents tPSA -2.91 to 79.15, WLOGP 0.40 to 5.96 vs paper's "tPSA ranges between -2.9 and 79.1 A2 and WLOGP between 0.4 and 6.0". Both match.

Normalised-space parameters (also published, SI Data S1/S2), if you prefer the foci form: HIA x1 0.711, y1 2.736, x2 1.405, y2 -0.720, d 4.052. BBB x1 0.978, y1 3.261, x2 1.098, y2 0.664, d 3.428. Normalisation was towards the standard deviation of each descriptor.
methods.reported_accuracy:
HIA / white ellipse: TP 547, TN 67, FP 26, FN 20, MCC = 0.7047, accuracy = 0.9303; 10-fold cross-validated MCC = 0.65, cross-validated accuracy 92%.
BBB / yolk ellipse: TP 151, TN 82, FP 22, FN 5, MCC = 0.7853, accuracy = 0.8962; 10-fold cross-validated MCC = 0.75, cross-validated accuracy 88%.
External illustration: 46 non-prodrug FDA NCEs, "a classification accuracy reaching 83%".
methods.accuracy_dataset: HIA-dataset: 660 small molecules, 567 well-absorbed (HIA+, fraction absorbed > 30%) and 93 poorly absorbed. BBB-dataset: 260 molecules, 156 permeant and 104 non-permeant (threshold log BB = 0). Both curated from literature with prodrugs, salts, molecules without polar atoms and suspected active-transport substrates REMOVED, then neutralised, aromatised, stereochemistry stripped.
methods.applicability_domain: Passive permeation of neutral, standardised small molecules. Actively transported and effluxed compounds were deliberately excluded from both training sets, so the model is undefined for them. Both datasets are drug-sized; nothing multi-kDa is in either. Descriptors must be computed as the authors did: WLOGP = Wildman-Crippen SMARTS fragmental logP (they implemented the 142 published fragments via OpenBabel), tPSA = Ertl fragment-based topological PSA.
methods.implementation_route: Implement directly, ~15 lines. RDKit's Crippen.MolLogP IS the Wildman-Crippen method and MolSurf.TPSA is Ertl's tPSA, so RDKit reproduces the authors' descriptors. Cross-check I ran: metoprolol gives RDKit WLOGP 1.61 and TPSA 50.72, identical to the values shown for metoprolol in Figure 1E of the ADMET-AI paper, and it falls inside both ellipses as expected for a CNS-penetrant beta-blocker. Reference implementation at /private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-seunghojung-Documents-DeepMind-Bio/a981ed0e-7f93-4115-84a0-d516f5c26372/scratchpad/verify.py

methods.name: Fsp3 (fraction sp3)
methods.paper: Lovering F, Bikker J, Humblet C. "Escape from flatland: increasing saturation as an approach to improving clinical success." J Med Chem 2009;52(21):6752-6756.
methods.equation: Verbatim from the abstract: "carbon bond saturation as defined by fraction sp(3) (Fsp(3)) where Fsp(3) = (number of sp(3) hybridized carbons/total carbon count)". Second measure: "simply whether a chiral carbon exists in the molecule".
methods.coefficients: No threshold is published as a rule. The paper reports a monotonic trend: mean Fsp3 rises from discovery compounds through clinical phases to marketed drugs. The frequently quoted 'Fsp3 >= 0.42' is a distributional observation about marketed drugs, NOT a cutoff stated as a rule. If you use a threshold, label it as a convention, not as Lovering's rule.
methods.reported_accuracy: No classifier metric. The paper demonstrates correlation of Fsp3 and chirality with progression from discovery to drug, and correlation of saturation with measured aqueous solubility.
methods.accuracy_dataset: Compounds spanning discovery, clinical phases 1-3, and marketed drugs; solubility correlation on an internal Wyeth dataset.
methods.applicability_domain: Small organic molecules. Degenerate cases: Fsp3 is undefined for a carbon-free molecule, and for a polypeptide it is dominated by backbone alpha-carbons and side-chain composition — it returns a high, uninformative value unrelated to the 'escape from flatland' argument.
methods.implementation_route: RDKit: rdMolDescriptors.CalcFractionCSP3(mol). Chirality: len(Chem.FindMolChiralCenters(mol, includeUnassigned=True)) > 0.

methods.name: Aromatic ring count
methods.paper: Ritchie TJ, Macdonald SJF. "The impact of aromatic ring count on compound developability - are too many aromatic rings a liability in drug design?" Drug Discov Today 2009;14(21-22):1011-1020.
methods.equation:
Count of aromatic + heteroaromatic rings. Verbatim conclusion from the abstract: "the fewer aromatic rings contained in an oral drug candidate, the more developable that candidate is probably to be; in addition, more than three aromatic rings in a molecule correlates with poorer compound developability and, thus, an increased risk of attrition in development."

Operational heuristic: aromatic ring count <= 3.
methods.coefficients: Threshold 3 aromatic rings.
methods.reported_accuracy: No classifier metric. Trend analysis against aqueous solubility, lipophilicity, serum albumin binding, CYP450 inhibition and hERG inhibition. The paper also shows that "even within a defined lipophilicity range, increased aromatic ring count leads to decreased aqueous solubility."
methods.accuracy_dataset: GSK internal developability assay datasets.
methods.applicability_domain: Oral small-molecule drug candidates.
methods.implementation_route: RDKit: rdMolDescriptors.CalcNumAromaticRings(mol). Beware: QED's AROM descriptor uses a different, non-equivalent definition (SSSR after deleting aliphatic rings) — do not mix them.

methods.name: ADMET-AI
methods.paper: Swanson K, Walther P, Leitz J, Mukherjee S, Wu JC, Shivnaraine RV, Zou J. "ADMET-AI: a machine learning ADMET platform for evaluation of large-scale chemical libraries." Bioinformatics 2024;40(7):btae416. Open access; I retrieved and read the full PDF.
methods.equation:
Not a closed-form equation. Architecture, verbatim: "ADMET-AI uses a deep learning model architecture for ADMET prediction called Chemprop-RDKit (available in Chemprop, v1.6.1) (Yang et al. 2019). Chemprop-RDKit consists of a graph neural network called Chemprop that is augmented with 200 physicochemical molecular features that are computed by the cheminformatics package RDKit (v2023.3.3)." Directed message-passing over the molecular graph, molecule embedding concatenated with the 200 RDKit features, then a feed-forward head.

Ensembling, verbatim: "For each TDC dataset, one Chemprop-RDKit model was trained for each of the five train/validation/test splits... At inference time, for each dataset, the average prediction is computed from an ensemble of models containing the five models trained on the five splits of that dataset." This is a 5-member ensemble MEAN. It is NOT a calibrated uncertainty estimate.

Multi-task setup, verbatim: "from the 41 ADMET datasets, two multi-task datasets were created, one containing all 10 regression datasets and one containing all 31 classification datasets. This enables the training of just two models (one regression, one classification) that cover all 41 ADMET properties." The two multi-task models are what the web server and package deploy.
methods.coefficients: 41 TDC ADMET datasets (TDC v0.4.1): 10 regression + 31 classification. 22 of them (9 regression, 13 classification) form the TDC ADMET Leaderboard. The package also computes 11 RDKit physicochemical properties (MW, logP, HBA, HBD, Lipinski violations, QED, stereocentres, TPSA, PAINS/BRENK/NIH alert counts), so the UI shows 52 rows total. DrugBank reference set for percentile contextualisation: 2579 approved drugs (DrugBank v5.1.10) per the paper; the current repo file ships 2845 rows, so the two differ — check which you are using.
methods.reported_accuracy:
Aggregate, verbatim: "an R2 > 0.6 for five of the ten regression datasets and an AUROC ... > 0.85 for 20 of the 31 classification datasets" (single-task models); best average rank on the 22-dataset TDC Leaderboard (rank 4 vs ContextPred 6, Chemprop 6, AttrMasking 6, RDKit2D+MLP 7, AttentiveFP 8, NeuralFP 9, GCN 9, Basic ML 10, Morgan+MLP 10, CNN 11).

methods.accuracy_dataset: Therapeutics Data Commons v0.4.1, per-dataset SCAFFOLD splits, 5 splits each; metrics are the mean over the 5 test splits. Dataset sizes as listed above.
methods.applicability_domain: NOT STATED BY THE AUTHORS. The paper contains no applicability-domain analysis, no per-prediction confidence intervals, and no out-of-distribution detection. The only contextualisation offered is a percentile against the DrugBank approved reference set, which the authors describe as interpretive context, explicitly not an uncertainty estimate. The de facto domain is the union of the 41 TDC training sets: drug-like small molecules. I computed the MW distribution of the shipped DrugBank reference (n=2845): median 334 Da, p75 447 Da, p95 811 Da, p99 1559 Da, p99.9 3562 Da, max 4610 Da; only 0.39% is >= 2000 Da and 0.035% is >= 4000 Da.
methods.implementation_route: pip install admet-ai (import name admet_ai). CLI: admet_predict --data_path /path/to/smiles.csv. Python: from admet_ai import ADMETModel; model = ADMETModel(); model.predict(smiles="CCO"). CPU-only works. CRITICAL VERSION TRAP, from the repo README: "This repo contains ADMET-AI v2, whereas our paper and the ADMET-AI live web server are based on ADMET-AI v1. The main difference is that ADMET-AI v2 uses Chemprop v2 (without RDKit fingerprints)... since the models were retrained from scratch, the predictions of ADMET-AI v2 will not exactly match those of ADMET-AI v1." The per-endpoint accuracies above were measured on v1. Pin admet_ai==1.4.0 (commit 9c84308) if you want the published numbers to apply; otherwise re-benchmark.

methods.name: Chemprop (D-MPNN)
methods.paper: Yang K, Swanson K, Jin W, et al. "Analyzing learned molecular representations for property prediction." J Chem Inf Model 2019;59(8):3370-3388.
methods.equation: Directed message-passing neural network over the molecular graph; molecule-level readout optionally concatenated with 200 RDKit 2D descriptors ('Chemprop-RDKit'), then a feed-forward head. I did NOT retrieve the message-passing update equations from the primary paper in this pass — treat the architecture description as summary-level, not transcribed.
methods.coefficients: Not applicable — weights are learned. Hyperparameters are per-dataset and live in the ADMET-AI reproduction scripts (scripts/train_tdc_admet_all.py in the repo).
methods.reported_accuracy: Not transcribed here. For ADMET purposes the relevant numbers are the ADMET-AI per-endpoint values above, which ARE Chemprop-RDKit numbers. Note that plain Chemprop (without RDKit features) sits at average rank 6 on the TDC ADMET Leaderboard vs ADMET-AI's rank 4.
methods.accuracy_dataset: TDC ADMET Leaderboard (22 datasets) for the ADMET-relevant comparison.
methods.applicability_domain: Whatever you train it on. Chemprop itself makes no domain claim and provides no AD estimate.
methods.implementation_route: pip install chemprop. This is the only defensible route to a peptide ADMET model out of this stack: retrain on peptide data you actually have. Chemprop v2 has a different API from v1; ADMET-AI v1 pins Chemprop v1.6.1.

methods.name: TDC benchmark harness / DeepPurpose
methods.paper: Huang K, Fu T, Gao W, et al. "Therapeutics Data Commons: machine learning datasets and tasks for drug discovery and development." NeurIPS Datasets and Benchmarks 2021. DeepPurpose: Huang K, Fu T, Glass LM, et al. Bioinformatics 2021;36(22-23):5545-5547.
methods.equation: Not applicable — TDC is a data/benchmark harness, DeepPurpose is a drug-target-interaction library.
methods.coefficients: TDC ADMET Benchmark Group = 22 datasets, all SCAFFOLD split, metrics transcribed from tdcommons.ai/benchmark/admet_group/overview: Caco2_Wang MAE; HIA_Hou AUROC; Pgp_Broccatelli AUROC; Bioavailability_Ma AUROC; Lipophilicity_AstraZeneca MAE; Solubility_AqSolDB MAE; BBB_Martins AUROC; PPBR_AZ MAE; VDss_Lombardo Spearman; CYP2C9_Veith AUPRC; CYP2D6_Veith AUPRC; CYP3A4_Veith AUPRC; CYP2C9_Substrate_CarbonMangels AUPRC; CYP2D6_Substrate_CarbonMangels AUPRC; CYP3A4_Substrate_CarbonMangels AUROC; Half_Life_Obach Spearman; Clearance_Hepatocyte_AZ Spearman; Clearance_Microsome_AZ Spearman; LD50_Zhu MAE; hERG AUROC; AMES AUROC; DILI AUROC.
methods.reported_accuracy: TDC supplies data and splits, not a model. DeepPurpose is a DTI library, not an ADMET predictor; it appears on TDC leaderboards as a baseline. Do not represent DeepPurpose as an ADMET model.
methods.accuracy_dataset: See per-dataset numbers under ADMET-AI.
methods.applicability_domain: Small molecules.
methods.implementation_route: pip install PyTDC to fetch datasets and the OFFICIAL splits — this is what you need to re-benchmark any model honestly. pip install DeepPurpose only if you actually want drug-target interaction.

methods.name: hERG-specific models
methods.paper: (a) TDC hERG benchmark as scored by ADMET-AI/Chemprop-RDKit. (b) Cai C, Guo P, Zhou Y, et al. "Deep Learning-Based Prediction of Drug-Induced Cardiotoxicity." J Chem Inf Model 2019;59(3):1073-1084 (deephERG). (c) Kim H, Park M, Lee I, Nam H. "BayeshERG: a robust, reliable and interpretable deep learning model for predicting hERG channel blockers." Brief Bioinform 2022;23(4):bbac211.
methods.equation: Not closed-form. (b) deephERG = multitask deep neural network on molecular descriptors/fingerprints, outperforming single-task DNN, naive Bayes, SVM, RF and GCNN in that paper. (c) BayeshERG = graph neural network with Bayesian inference via Monte Carlo dropout plus global multihead attentive pooling, with transfer learning pre-training on 300,000 compounds — the abstract states they "implemented a Bayesian neural network with Monte Carlo dropout to calibrate the uncertainty of the prediction".
methods.coefficients: Not applicable — learned weights.
methods.reported_accuracy:
(a) ADMET-AI on TDC hERG: AUROC 0.8388, AUPRC 0.9062, mean over 5 scaffold splits (from the shipped admet.csv).
(b) deephERG, verbatim from the abstract: "the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) value for the best model of deephERG is 0.967 on the validation set." This is an INTERNAL validation number and is not comparable to the 0.839 scaffold-split figure.
(c) BayeshERG: the abstract claims it "outperformed predictive performance and uncertainty calibration performance" versus most publicly available hERG models on internal and external validation, with in vitro confirmation, but states no headline AUROC. AUROC NOT RETRIEVED for BayeshERG (paper not open access).
Context: Ritchie & Macdonald 2009 found aromatic ring count correlates with hERG inhibition, and Gleeson 2008 lists hERG inhibition among the assays that deteriorate with increasing MW/logP.
methods.accuracy_dataset: (a) TDC hERG, 648 compounds, scaffold split. (b) deephERG: 7,889 compounds with well-defined experimental hERG data, plus application to 1,824 FDA-approved drugs (29.6% flagged as potential hERG inhibitors). (c) BayeshERG: 300,000-compound pre-training corpus plus internal and external hERG validation sets (sizes not retrieved).
methods.applicability_domain: All three are trained exclusively on small-molecule hERG patch-clamp / binding data. The 648-compound TDC set is small and heavily drug-biased. AUROC 0.84 on 648 scaffold-split small molecules conveys essentially nothing about anything structurally unlike those 648 molecules.
methods.implementation_route: hERG comes free inside ADMET-AI (endpoint id 'hERG'). BayeshERG source at github.com/GIST-CSBL/BayeshERG. deephERG has no maintained public package I verified. For a peptide, the honest route to cardiac safety is an in vitro hERG patch-clamp assay, not any of these.

methods.name: Conformal prediction / CPSign (calibrated uncertainty)
methods.paper: Arvidsson McShane S, Norinder U, Alvarsson J, Ahlberg E, Carlsson L, Spjuth O. "CPSign: conformal prediction for cheminformatics modeling." J Cheminform 2024;16:75. Open access (CC BY); I fetched and read the full text. Foundational method: Norinder U, Carlsson L, Boyer S, Eklund M. "Introducing Conformal Prediction in Predictive Modeling. A Transparent and Flexible Alternative to Applicability Domain Determination." J Chem Inf Model 2014;54(6):1596-1603 (NOT open access; full text not retrieved). Overview: Alvarsson J, Arvidsson McShane S, Norinder U, Spjuth O. "Predicting With Confidence: Using Conformal Prediction in Drug Discovery." J Pharm Sci 2021 (PMID 33075380).
methods.equation:
Inductive conformal prediction, transcribed verbatim from the CPSign paper:

"...the nonconformity, alpha_(n+1), is calculated and then ranked against the list alpha_1,...,alpha_(n+1) (i.e., including the n+1 test instance) according to Eq. 1, resulting in a p-value for the object."

  p_(n+1) = |{ j = 1,...,n+1 : alpha_j >= alpha_(n+1) }| / (n + 1)

MONDRIAN (class-conditional) variant, verbatim: "This ranking is in most cases performed separately (referred to as mondrian) for each possible class label y (i.e., with a separate list of alpha values for each class). The resulting prediction of a test-object is a set of p-values, one for each possible class label. These p-values can then be subjected to a statistical test in order to obtain a set-prediction, i.e. if we wish to have 90% confidence in the prediction we specify a significance level, epsilon, of 0.1 and have to include all labels with a p-value equal to or higher than 0.1 in the prediction set. The resulting prediction sets can thus be empty (no classes predicted), single-label (informative) or multi-label (less informative)."

This is exactly the machinery the platform needs: at 1 - epsilon confidence the output is a SET, and an empty or full set is the model saying it does not know.

Critical caveat stated by the CPSign authors: "this guarantee may in practice be difficult to achieve sometimes due to assay drifts or in case data splitting is performed in a non-random way (such as scaffold-splitting). The validity is thus commonly assessed by calculating the error rate for a set of significance levels, or by plotting a calibration curve of error rate vs significance level."
methods.coefficients: No fitted coefficients — conformal prediction is a wrapper. Tunables: significance level epsilon; Mondrian conditioning on the class label; choice of nonconformity measure. For regression the output is a prediction interval rather than a set. CPSign also implements transductive CP and Venn-ABERS probabilistic prediction.
inputs_required: A held-out proper calibration set drawn exchangeably with the test data
methods.reported_accuracy: Validity IS the guarantee, not an accuracy figure: at significance epsilon the long-run error rate is <= epsilon, provided exchangeability holds. CPSign reports "robust predictive performance with comparative predictive efficiency, with superior runtime and lower hardware requirements compared to neural network based models" versus random forest and a D-MPNN. Efficiency (fraction of single-label sets) is the quality metric and must be reported alongside validity.
methods.accuracy_dataset: Multiple cheminformatics benchmarks in the CPSign paper. Related published applications: conformal logD regression on ~1.6 M ACD/logD compounds (PMC5882484); Mondrian cross-conformal on large imbalanced bioactivity sets (PMID 28628322); Mondrian CP for toxicity endpoints (PMC9822478), which reports that "the class imbalance problem is gracefully handled through the use of Mondrian conformal prediction without the use of over- and/or under-sampling, weighting of classes or cost-sensitive methods".
methods.applicability_domain: Conformal prediction is the correct AD mechanism to bolt on — Norinder et al. 2014 present it precisely as "a transparent and flexible alternative to applicability domain determination". BUT the exchangeability assumption fails hard for a 4 kDa polycationic peptide scored against a small-molecule calibration set. In that regime the coverage guarantee does not hold and conformal prediction will return an over-confident interval. It is not a substitute for refusing to predict out of domain.
methods.implementation_route: CPSign (Java, github.com/arosbio/cpsign, open source) for a complete SVM-based conformal stack. In Python: crepes, nonconformist, or MAPIE will wrap any sklearn/torch predictor. ADMET-AI ships NO conformal layer — you must add one, with a calibration set drawn from your actual chemotype.

admet.recommendation:
WHAT TO IMPLEMENT, IN PRIORITY ORDER

Tier 1 — exact equations verified against primary sources, safe to compute for small molecules:
  1. CNS MPO. Breakpoints read directly off Figure 1 of Wager 2016 (which reprints the 2010 figure): ClogP 3/5, ClogD 2/4, MW 360/500, TPSA 20/40/90/120 hump, HBD 0.5/3.5 (see the HBD note — the naive 0/4 line does NOT reproduce the paper's plotted points), pKa 8/10. Equal weights, sum 0-6. One blocker: ClogD(7.4) and most-basic pKa are not in RDKit; you must name whichever external calculator you use, because the 2016 authors themselves report the score moves substantially with it. Also print the independent AUC 0.61 next to the score so nobody reads 4.7/6 as a probability.
  2. BOILED-Egg. Fully parameterised and verified: HIA ellipse centre (71.051, 2.292), major 142.081, minor 8.740, angle -1.031325 deg; BBB ellipse centre (38.117, 3.177), major 82.061, minor 5.557, angle -0.171887 deg, in the (tPSA, WLOGP) plane. RDKit's Crippen.MolLogP and MolSurf.TPSA are exactly the descriptors the authors used — confirmed by metoprolol giving WLOGP 1.61 / TPSA 50.72, matching published values. Report the published MCC and accuracy with every call: HIA MCC 0.7047 / acc 0.9303 (CV MCC 0.65, CV acc 92%); BBB MCC 0.7853 / acc 0.8962 (CV MCC 0.75, CV acc 88%).
  3. QED and SAscore. Both already installed as reference implementations: rdkit.Chem.QED (ADS parameters and the wmean weight vector are in QED.py and match the paper; the three published anchor molecules reproduce to 3 dp) and rdkit/Contrib/SA_Score/sascorer.py. Do not hand-roll either.
  4. Lipinski, Veber, Ghose, Pfizer 3/75, Fsp3, aromatic ring count. All transcribed from primary abstracts with exact cutoffs. Report Pfizer 3/75 as a quadrant plus its ~2.5x odds ratio, never as a toxicity probability.

Tier 2 — implement only with an explicit provenance disclaimer:
  Egan, Muegge, GSK 4/400. For all three I could NOT retrieve the primary numeric definition (all three are paywalled with no OA copy on Unpaywall). The circulating cutoffs (Egan WLOGP <= 5.88 / TPSA <= 131.6; Muegge's nine-criterion set; MW 400 / logP 4) are SwissADME-lineage operationalisations or folklore. If you ship them, label them as such in the UI and in code comments. Marking them "transcribed from Egan 2000" would be exactly the failure mode you are trying to eliminate.
  Do NOT implement CNS MPO_V2 — that paper was retracted (noted in the Molecules 2024 review, ref 30).

Tier 3 — the ML layer:
  pip install admet-ai gives 41 endpoints on CPU at roughly 0.018 s/molecule (8 cores, 1 M molecules in ~5 h; 3.1 h with 32 cores + GPU; 28.1 h via the web server). Two traps: (a) the pip package is v2 (Chemprop v2, RDKit fingerprints removed, retrained from scratch) while every published accuracy is v1 — pin admet_ai==1.4.0 if you want the numbers to be true, or re-benchmark; (b) two of the ten regression endpoints have NEGATIVE R2 on scaffold split (VDss_Lombardo R2 = -1.21, Half_Life_Obach R2 = -2.39, from the package's own admet.csv). Those are worse than predicting the training mean. Suppress them, or show the training-set mean with an explicit "no signal" flag. Several classification endpoints are also weak despite respectable AUROC — CYP2C9_Substrate is AUROC 0.628 / AUPRC 0.370, Tox21 SR-ATAD5 is AUROC 0.879 / AUPRC 0.312.

Nothing in this stack provides calibrated uncertainty out of the box. ADMET-AI's 5-model ensemble mean is variance reduction, not calibration, and its DrugBank percentile is interpretive context the authors never claim is an uncertainty estimate. For intervals with a coverage guarantee you must add a conformal layer yourself (crepes / MAPIE / nonconformist in Python, or CPSign), using Mondrian class-conditional calibration for the imbalanced toxicity endpoints — and you need a calibration set drawn from your actual chemotype, which for peptides you do not have.

HOW TO REPORT AN ADMET PREDICTION

Every emitted prediction should carry six fields, not one number:
  1. Point estimate WITH units and the direction of the scale.
  2. An interval or a prediction set with a stated coverage level. For conformal classification: "at 90% confidence the prediction set is {blocker, non-blocker}" — which honestly says nothing is known — or a regression interval [a, b] at 1 - epsilon. A bare point estimate is not acceptable because per-compound error is nowhere near constant: the same platform that gets Caco-2 to R2 0.71 gets half-life to R2 -2.39, and a user shown "t1/2 = 6.2 h" has no way to tell those regimes apart.
  3. The endpoint's benchmark performance ON THE DATASET IT WAS MEASURED ON, named, with the split type. "hERG AUROC 0.839 (TDC hERG, n=648, mean over 5 scaffold splits)" — not "hERG AUROC 0.839". The dataset and split change the number a lot: deephERG reports AUC 0.967 on its internal validation of 7,889 compounds while ADMET-AI reports 0.839 on the 648-compound TDC scaffold split. Both are correct; quoting either without its dataset is not.
  4. An applicability-domain verdict: IN DOMAIN / MARGINAL / OUT OF DOMAIN, with the criterion used (nearest-neighbour Tanimoto to training set, descriptor-space distance, or conformal p-value), and REFUSAL to emit a number when out of domain.
  5. Provenance: model version, training-data version, descriptor calculator. ADMET-AI v1 vs v2 give different numbers for the same SMILES.
  6. Whether the value is a prediction, a rule-based heuristic score, or a computed descriptor. CNS MPO is not a prediction. QED is not a prediction. Conflating them with a model output at AUROC 0.84 is a category error users make constantly.

DOME (Walsh I, Fishman D, Garcia-Gasulla D, et al., "DOME: recommendations for supervised machine learning validation in biology," Nat Methods 2021;18:1122-1127, doi 10.1038/s41592-021-01205-4; open preprint arXiv:2006.16189, which I read) is the right standard to cite and it applies directly. Its four sections are Data, Optimization, Model, Evaluation. The items that bite hardest here, quoted from Box 1:
  - Data / Redundancy between data splits: "How were the sets split? Are the training and test sets independent? How was this enforced (e.g. redundancy reduction to less than X% pairwise identity)?" — this is why scaffold split matters and why random-split hERG AUCs in the literature are not comparable to TDC numbers.
  - Model / Execution time: "How much real-time does a single representative prediction require on a standard machine?"
  - Evaluation / Comparison: "Was a comparison to publicly available methods performed on benchmark datasets? Was a comparison to simpler baselines performed?" — for VDss and half-life the mean-predictor baseline BEATS the model, which is precisely why the baseline requirement exists.
  - Evaluation / Confidence: "Do the performance metrics have confidence intervals? Are the results statistically significant to claim that the method is superior to others and baselines?"
  DOME Table 1 lists this last item as a REQUIREMENT (bold in the original), not a recommendation: "Confidence intervals/error intervals and statistical tests to gauge prediction robustness. (requirement)". A platform emitting bare point estimates is non-compliant with DOME on a required item.
  Also adopt the DOME registry / DOME-ML annotation wizard so each model card in the platform is a filled-in DOME record rather than prose.

For the QSAR side specifically, the older but still-binding standard is the OECD Principles for the Validation of (Q)SAR Models: principle 3 is "a defined domain of applicability" and principle 4 is "appropriate measures of goodness-of-fit, robustness and predictivity". A tool that predicts hERG for a peptide violates principle 3 by construction.
warnings: PEPTIDE APPLICABILITY — THE HEADLINE. Your candidates are multi-kDa polycationic peptides. Essentially NOTHING in this document applies to them, and the platform must say so rather than emit a number. Concretely: every one of the 41 TDC ADMET training sets is a small-molecule set (largest 13,130 CYP2D6 compounds), and the ADMET-AI DrugBank reference set that contextualises its output (which I downloaded and analysed, n=2845) has median MW 334 Da, p75 447, p95 811, p99 1559, p99.9 3562, max 4610 Da; only 0.39% is >= 2000 Da. A 4 kDa peptide sits beyond the 99.9th percentile of even that reference. There is no defensible sense in which a Chemprop message-passing network trained on 648 drug-like molecules extrapolates to a 35-residue polycation.

ENDPOINTS THAT ARE SIMPLY NOT PREDICTABLE FOR A MULTI-kDa POLYCATIONIC PEPTIDE — refuse, do not estimate: (1) hERG blockade. The TDC hERG model is 648 small molecules; hERG block by small molecules is a lipophilic-amine pore-binding pharmacophore that does not describe a 4 kDa polycation, and peptide cardiac liabilities run through entirely different mechanisms. Applying it is out of domain by every criterion. (2) CYP1A2/2C9/2C19/2D6/3A4 inhibition and substrate status — peptides are cleared by proteases and renal filtration, not CYP; the question is malformed, not merely hard. (3) Caco-2 / PAMPA / HIA / oral bioavailability — passive transcellular permeation models with no poorly-permeable peptides in training. (4) BBB penetration by ANY method here — BBB_Martins (n=1975 small molecules); the BOILED-Egg yolk ellipse spans WLOGP 0.4-6.0 and tPSA up to 79 A^2, and a 4 kDa peptide has tPSA in the many hundreds, i.e. outside the plot entirely; and CNS MPO, whose MW transform saturates at 0 above 500 Da so every peptide scores 0 on MW, 0 on TPSA and usually 0 on HBD — a structurally guaranteed low score carrying no information. (5) VDss and half-life — already negative R2 for small molecules; for peptides they are noise. (6) P-gp inhibition, LD50_Zhu, Tox21 panels, AMES, DILI — all small-molecule training sets containing no polycationic peptides.

PROPERTIES THAT DEGRADE TO MEANINGLESSNESS RATHER THAN FAILING LOUDLY — the dangerous ones, because they still return a plausible-looking float. Crippen/Wildman logP is an atom-contribution model with no ionisation term; for a molecule with many permanently charged side chains at pH 7.4 it returns something that is not a logP in any physical sense. RDKit TPSA is an additive fragment sum validated on drug-like molecules; summing it over 35 residues gives a large number with no validated relationship to permeability. 'pKa of the most basic centre' is ill-defined for a polycation with many basic sites of coupled, sequence-dependent pKa — CNS MPO's sixth term is therefore undefined, not merely uncertain. QED returns a near-zero value purely because MW and PSA are off the ends of ADS curves fitted to 771 oral drugs; that near-zero is an artefact. SAscore saturates near 10 from the size penalty even though the peptide is routine by SPPS. Fsp3 returns a high value dominated by backbone alpha-carbons, unrelated to the 'escape from flatland' argument. Emit these as descriptors with an explicit out-of-domain flag, or not at all.

PROVENANCE GAPS I COULD NOT CLOSE — do not let these turn into invented numbers. Egan 2000 (10.1021/jm000292e): the PSA/AlogP98 confidence-ellipse parameters were NOT retrieved (paywalled, no OA copy). Muegge 2001 (10.1021/jm015507e): the pharmacophore-point criteria table was NOT retrieved. Gleeson 2008 (10.1021/jm701122q): the '4/400' numbers were NOT found in any text I read. BayeshERG's headline AUROC was NOT retrieved. Chemprop's message-passing equations were NOT transcribed. Lipinski's original PDF was not retrieved, though the abstract states the rule verbatim and is sufficient. Everything flagged equation_retrieved=false or verified=false falls into this bucket.

CNS MPO HBD IS THE MOST LIKELY IMPLEMENTATION BUG. Figure 1E labels the arrows 0 and 4, but the plotted desirability values are 1.00 / 0.83 / 0.50 / 0.17 / 0.00 for HBD 0-4. Implementing the line literally from (0,1) to (4,0) yields 1.00 / 0.75 / 0.50 / 0.25 / 0.00 and silently disagrees with the paper for every molecule with 1 or 3 donors. Use g=0.5, r=3.5. I verified the corrected form reproduces the published points exactly.

CNS MPO_V2 WAS RETRACTED. The Molecules 2024 review (29:1264) states the MPO_V2 paper was retracted. Several CNS MPO implementations in the wild (including the widely-linked GitHub script sdecesco/CNS_MPO) compute an 'MPOScore_v2' alongside the real score. Do not ship it.

ADMET-AI VERSION MISMATCH. The pip package today is v2 (Chemprop v2, RDKit fingerprints removed, models retrained from scratch); every performance figure in the Bioinformatics paper and every number in the shipped admet.csv was measured on v1. The maintainers state explicitly that v2 predictions 'will not exactly match those of ADMET-AI v1'. Pin admet_ai==1.4.0 (commit 9c84308) if you intend to cite the published accuracies, or re-run the benchmark. Also: the paper says the DrugBank reference is 2579 approved drugs (v5.1.10) but the repo file has 2845 rows — the percentiles you display depend on which you load.

NEGATIVE R^2 ENDPOINTS MUST NOT BE DISPLAYED AS PREDICTIONS. From ADMET-AI's own shipped metrics file: VDss_Lombardo R2 = -1.2107 and Half_Life_Obach R2 = -2.3857 on scaffold split. Negative R2 means the model is worse than the constant mean predictor. Showing 'predicted half-life: 6.2 h' is strictly worse than the hardcoded number it replaces, because it looks computed. Suppress, or show the training mean labelled 'no predictive signal'.

AUROC HIDES CLASS-IMBALANCE FAILURE. Several ADMET-AI classification endpoints pair acceptable AUROC with unusable AUPRC: CYP2C9_Substrate AUROC 0.628 / AUPRC 0.370; Tox21 SR-ATAD5 AUROC 0.879 / AUPRC 0.312; NR-PPAR-gamma AUROC 0.916 / AUPRC 0.439; NR-Aromatase AUROC 0.906 / AUPRC 0.475; NR-ER AUROC 0.749 / AUPRC 0.458. Report both, and prefer AUPRC for the rare-positive toxicity endpoints, as TDC itself does for the CYP-inhibition and CYP-substrate leaderboards.

CONFORMAL PREDICTION IS NOT A LICENCE TO PREDICT OUT OF DOMAIN. Its coverage guarantee rests on exchangeability between calibration and test data. The CPSign authors state the guarantee 'may in practice be difficult to achieve sometimes due to assay drifts or in case data splitting is performed in a non-random way (such as scaffold-splitting)'. Calibrating on small molecules and then scoring a 4 kDa peptide breaks exchangeability outright — you get a confident-looking interval with no validity behind it. Conformal prediction is the right tool for graded uncertainty INSIDE the domain; it is not a way to keep emitting numbers outside it.

DESCRIPTOR-CALCULATOR DEPENDENCE IS A REAL SOURCE OF DISAGREEMENT, NOT A ROUNDING ISSUE. The Wager 2016 authors report CNS MPO 'can vary substantially depending on the computational software and method used to calculate physiochemical properties (mainly LogD and pKa)'. RDKit's own QED docstring notes its values differ from the original publication because of logP calculator differences. HBA has at least three incompatible definitions in play (Lipinski N+O count, RDKit CalcNumHBA, QED's 11-SMARTS set) and aromatic ring count has two (CalcNumAromaticRings vs QED's SSSR-after-deletion). Pin and document one definition per descriptor and store it with every result.

THE HONEST POSITIVE PATH FOR PEPTIDES. None of the above means no ADMET assessment is possible — only that these small-molecule tools cannot supply it. Defensible substitutes: peptide-specific descriptors (net charge at pH 7.4, isoelectric point, GRAVY hydropathy, helical amphipathicity, aggregation propensity), protease-cleavage-site prediction, serum- and plasma-stability assays, renal-clearance reasoning from size and charge, immunogenicity/MHC-binding prediction, and — for cardiac safety and BBB penetration specifically — in vitro hERG patch clamp and an in vivo Kp,uu measurement, because there is no validated in silico route for a polycationic peptide. If you want an ML model, retrain Chemprop on peptide data you actually have; do not extrapolate one trained on 648 small molecules.

errors.item: ESM Atlas fold API — root-cause diagnosis
errors.claimed: 'HARD FINDING — THE API IS ALIVE AT THE GATEWAY BUT ITS INFERENCE BACKEND IS DEAD... I sent novel random sequences at lengths 10, 20, 30, 50, 80, 120, 200 — ALL returned HTTP 504... The ONLY 200 I ever got was for the trivial string MKTVRQERLK... i.e. a cached result from an earlier user. Conclusion: only pre-cached sequences succeed; anything novel times out.'
errors.actual: FALSIFIED. A novel random 10-mer KETSWGRLWD returned HTTP 200 in 25.04 s with 90 ATOM records — a genuine fold, not a cache hit. Re-POSTing the same sequence immediately after returned HTTP 200 in 0.64 s, proving my own first call populated the cache. A brand-new 12-mer MDEVKWGHDHSR then returned 504 at 29.08 s. The backend is NOT dead: it computes, but slowly, and the binding constraint is the ~29 s AWS API Gateway timeout, so only very short sequences finish. The operational advice (do not build on it) survives, but the stated mechanism is wrong and the 'ALL returned HTTP 504' measurement is not reproducible. Everything else in this row reproduced exactly: 401 res -> 413 'Sequence is longer than 400.'; 400 res -> passes validation (then 504); empty -> 400 'Sequence is empty.'; bad chars -> 422 with the token set; GET -> 403 'Missing Authentication Token'; B-factors on residue 1 N/CA/C/CB/O = 0.83/0.82/0.83/0.78/0.76 (per-atom, 0-1 scale); REMARK 'ESM METAGENOMIC ATLAS DATA IS AVAILABLE UNDER A CC-BY-4.0 LICENSE FOR ACADEMIC AND COMMERCIAL USE.'

errors.item: CNS MPO — sensitivity to ClogD/pKa calculator, attributed to Wager 2016
errors.claimed: "Score is highly sensitive to which ClogD and pKa calculator you use — the 2016 authors say so themselves" and "you must name whichever external calculator you use, because the 2016 authors themselves report the score moves substantially with it."
errors.actual: INVERTED ATTRIBUTION. I retrieved the full Wager 2016 open-access PDF (pubs.acs.org/doi/pdf/10.1021/acschemneuro.6b00029?ref=article_openPDF; Unpaywall is_oa=true). The paper states the opposite: "Because of the utilization of piecewise linear transformation functions, we expected the CNS MPO score to be relatively insensitive to small variability in these modeled properties... when using the newer model calculations of ClogD and pKa to compute the CNS MPO desirability score, we observed very good correlation and small variances in the CNS MPO score (R2 = 0.94, slope = 0.96), consistent with our original objective of a robust algorithm (Figure 8C). The changes in CNS MPO desirability score resulting from the modified values of ClogD and pKa are all less than one unit." ACD v9.03 vs v12.1 shifted individual drugs by <1 unit on a 0-6 scale (Table 1: largest deltas 0.6-0.9). The practical advice (record which calculator you used) is sound; the attribution to the authors is a direct contradiction of the source and must be removed.

errors.item: CNS MPO peptide warning — completeness of the failure mode
errors.claimed: "CNS MPO, whose MW transform saturates at 0 above 500 Da so every peptide scores 0 on MW, 0 on TPSA and usually 0 on HBD — a structurally guaranteed low score carrying no information."
errors.actual: UNDER-WARNS. Computed with the verified breakpoints on three polycationic peptides (11-mer YGRKKRRQRRR, 4.5 kDa 35-mer, 12.6 kDa 96-mer): T0(MW)=0.00, T0(TPSA)=0.00, T0(HBD)=0.00 as claimed — but T0(ClogP)=1.00 in every case, because Crippen logP is -10.07 / -31.37 / -86.04 and the transform is one-sided (T0=1 for anything <=3). ClogD(7.4) will behave identically. So a polycationic peptide is guaranteed FULL marks on both lipophilicity terms for a physically meaningless reason, and can land near 3/6 rather than near 0 — a mid-range-looking score, which is more dangerous than the floored score the report describes. The report notes the one-sidedness abstractly ("trivially small fragments score 6") but never connects it to the peptide case.

APPLICABILITY DOMAIN — I confirm the report's headline as a HARD LIMIT, not a caveat, and can now substantiate it quantitatively. None of the cited models was trained on, or is mathematically defined over, chemical space containing 3-11 kDa polycationic peptides. (a) BOILED-Egg is bounded BY CONSTRUCTION at tPSA <= 142.1 A^2 (HIA) and <= 79.1 A^2 (BBB yolk); measured RDKit TPSA for a 4.5 kDa 35-mer polycation is 2350 A^2 and for a 12.6 kDa peptide 6448 A^2 — 16x to 80x outside the ellipse, and both training sets (660 and 260 molecules) had suspected active-transport substrates removed. (b) CNS MPO derives from 119 marketed CNS drugs of median MW 305.3 Da; its MW transform is identically zero above 500 Da, and its sixth term ('most basic pKa') is not merely uncertain but UNDEFINED for a polycation with many coupled, sequence-dependent basic sites. (c) Ghose caps at MW 480 and 70 total atoms; a 35-mer has >600 heavy atoms. (d) Lipinski's set is ~2245 WDI Phase-II orals with transporter substrates and named exception classes excluded; the abstract says nothing about peptides. (e) Egan's abstract states outliers 'were identified as being actively transported' and removed, putting transported species out of domain by construction. (f) ADMET-AI's 41 TDC datasets are small-molecule sets (largest CYP2D6_Veith n=13130; hERG n=648), and its DrugBank contextualisation set (n=2845, verified) has median MW 334 Da with only 0.387% at or above 2000 Da — a 4 kDa peptide sits past the 99.9th percentile of the reference set itself. (g) Conformal prediction cannot rescue any of this: exchangeability between a small-molecule calibration set and a polycationic peptide fails outright, which the CPSign authors' own caveat covers. Measured artefacts confirming the report's 'degrade to meaninglessness' warning: QED returns 0.0153-0.0164 for all three test peptides (ADS tail artefact); SAscore returns exactly 10.00 for the 35-mer and 96-mer (size-penalty saturation); Fsp3 returns 0.62-0.70 (backbone alpha-carbons); Crippen logP returns -10 to -86 (no ionisation term). The platform should refuse to emit these, not flag them.
